sw_strv_74: Built on the obsolete Strv m/42 chassis, the Strv 74 received an all-new turret carrying a high-velocity 75 mm gun adapted from the Lvkan m/37 anti-aircraft weapon, and served the Swedish Army from 1958 until 1984, latterly in infantry support. In the game it is made for hilly maps: deep gun depression lets it fight with only its small turret showing, and its APDS round, at about 247 mm of penetration up close, can defeat almost anything. The tall hull is a liability in towns, and weak mobility plus a slow reverse make retreating hard. It arrived in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_81: Sweden bought 240 Centurion Mk 3s in two batches in 1953 and 1955, the second with some Mk 5 features such as a bore-evacuated barrel, and as the Strv 81 they formed the core of its armoured units into the 2000s, later rebuilt as the Strv 102 and 104. In the game it plays much like an early main battle tank: a two-plane stabiliser lets it aim and fire on the move, and the 84 mm 20-pounder's APDS, at up to 384 mm of penetration, lets it take on heavy tanks directly. It came with Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_81_rb52: This Strv 81 trial vehicle carried RB 52 missiles, a Swedish-built copy of the French SS.11 wire-guided ATGM, at a time when many armies expected missiles to outrange tank guns; the army chose dedicated missile carriers instead and dropped the project. In the game it keeps the regular Strv 81's stabilised 20-pounder and adds three turret-mounted MCLOS missiles that penetrate up to 600 mm. They climb before levelling off, leaving a blind zone of up to about 200 m, so range matters when firing them. It was sold in the 8th Anniversary sale during the "Raining Fire" update, replacing the version once found in the British tree.
sw_strv_m31: Landsverk's L-10, known in Swedish service as the Strv m/31, was an advanced interwar design: the first tank built with an all-welded hull, with its crew looking out through periscopes rather than vision slits; only three were made. In the game it is quick but so thinly armoured that heavy machine guns can get through its sides and rear. Its strength is the 37 mm Bofors with the slpprj m/49 APDS round, which stays effective even against tanks like the B1 ter and Valentine, whereas its APHE shell struggles even against starter tanks. It joined the game in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_m38: Landsverk derived the Strv m/38 from its L-60 design, and as series L-60 S-I it was the first version Sweden adopted, before newer series took over from 1939. In the game it is a nimble light tank set apart by an APDS round, unusual at this early stage, which gives it the penetration to tackle much better-armoured opponents. It was part of the original Swedish ground tree in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_m39: Ordered in 1939 to fix the m/38's thin armour, the Strv m/39 ended up without the extra protection because Landsverk argued the hull and suspension could not carry the weight; it gained a revised turret with better fire control and lever steering instead. It plays much like the m/38: quick and well armed but fragile, with only three crew and armour that heavy machine guns can defeat. A fast reload, an APDS round that can beat even heavy tanks frontally, APHE for side shots and 14 degrees of gun depression make it a strong hull-down fighter. It arrived in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_m39_td: Twitch viewers could earn this second copy of the Strv m/39 in 2020 by watching War Thunder broadcasts. The real tank was meant to up-armour the m/38, but Landsverk said the chassis could not take it, so it mostly received a new turret with improved fire control and lever steering. In play it matches its relative: a fast-firing 37 mm with a potent APDS round and APHE for flank shots, plus 14 degrees of depression for ridge fighting, offset by armour that heavy machine guns can pierce and a crew of only three.
sw_strv_m40l: The Strv m/40L (L-60 S/III) followed the m/39 with thicker armour, a reshaped mantlet, a commander's cupola and side hatches, and it later formed the basis of Finland's L-62 Anti II anti-aircraft vehicle. Its armour fixes much of what held back the m/38 and m/39, keeping out autocannon fire and some 37-40 mm solid shot, while good mobility suits sniping and flanking. The APDS round can get through tanks as heavy as the B1 ter and the large crew absorbs hits, but HEAT from the M4A3 (105), Pz.IV E or StuG III A can wipe it out through overpressure. It came in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_m41_s1: In 1939 Sweden bought the rights to the Czech ČKD TNH, the export form of the LT-38, and the S-I was the initial batch of Strv m/41s made at home, recognisable by an extra periscope above the loader; deliveries ran from 1942 to 1943. Its armour is roughly on par with the Panzer III J and its mobility is decent, if behind the BT-7 or M5A1. The 37 mm kan m/38 reloads quickly and its APDS round can penetrate even heavy tanks, though the small calibre demands precise shots at crew or modules, so it works best supporting others. It was added in the "Ixwa Strike" update.
sw_strv_m41_s2: Licence-built by Scania-Vabis, the Strv m/41 S-II was the second Swedish series of the TNH (the Panzer 38(t) in German use), with armour thickened from 25 to 50 mm, a stronger L 603 engine and a slightly longer hull; 122 were ordered in 1942 and all later became Pbv 301 carriers. In play it resembles the Pz.38(t) F but adds a 37 mm APDS round with over 100 mm of flat penetration, enough to kill a B1 bis or M4A3 (105) with a well-placed first shot. Thin sides mean it should snipe at range rather than brawl. It arrived in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_m42_delat_torn: One of the more experimental Strv m/42 branches, the DT ("Delat Torn", or split turret) put an autoloading 75 mm gun in a turret divided in two to make room for the mechanism; a prototype followed in 1945 but was judged unsuccessful after 1946 trials and cancelled. Its standout trait in the game is a reload that can fall to around 3 seconds, backed by an ordinary APCBC round. Armour is light-tank thin and the exposed autoloader ammunition detonates easily, but reasonable mobility allows flanking and the gun depresses to -10 degrees. It came in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury".
sw_strv_m42_eh: Derived from the Lago I that Landsverk had built for Hungary, the Strv m/42 EH accounted for 57 of the 282 Strv m/42s ordered; obsolete on arrival, it was turned into the Ikv 73 infantry support vehicle in 1957. In the game it is a conventional medium tank whose best trait is generous gun depression, so it is strongest fighting hull-down over ridges near objectives or roads. The 75 mm struggles against angled armour and heavy tanks in uptiers, and a large silhouette with middling speed makes it a poor flanker. It was one of the Update 1.97 "Viking Fury" additions.
sw_t_28: Across the Winter and Continuation Wars, Finnish forces captured seven Soviet T-28s; these were the only ones that could move under their own power, since the Finns lacked tractors to recover the rest, which were stripped for parts. This Swedish-tree copy came with the "Fire and Ice" update and performs exactly like the Soviet T-28, except that it begins with weaker Sh-354T shrapnel rounds until the BR-305A APHE is researched. The large crew helps it shrug off autocannon fire, but they sit close together, so a 75 mm hit from an M3 Lee or short-barrelled Pz.IV F1 can take out several at once.
sw_t_34_1941: Finnish forces seized four 76 mm T-34s and Germany passed on three more, the first taken near the Lower Svir hydroelectric station in October 1941 after it got stuck on tree stumps; T-34s stayed Finland's most modern tanks until the late 1950s. Added to the Swedish tree in Update 2.21 "Fire and Ice", it handles like the Soviet original, with good cross-country mobility, decent armour and APHEBC shells that penetrate adequately and do heavy damage afterwards. The usual Soviet drawbacks remain: limited gun depression and a cramped crew layout.
sw_t_34_85_zis_53: Seven T-34-85s fell into Finnish hands at the Battle of Tali-Ihantala in summer 1944, though the two repaired for service were ready only in September, shortly before Finland left the war. It joined the Swedish tree in Update 2.21 "Fire and Ice" and is a balanced medium tank, quick enough to reach objectives early or flank, with an 85 mm ZiS-S-53 whose APHE lacks top-end penetration but usually kills in one hit. Hull armour is mediocre, although the rounded turret front can sometimes stop 76 mm or even 88 mm shells at medium range.
sw_t_50_fin: Finnish troops captured this rare Soviet light tank, one of around 50 built at Leningrad's Voroshilov Factory, near Petrozavodsk and fitted it with extra armour; it served as a company command tank until an engine failure in June 1944 put it out of action for good, and it now sits in the Parola Tank Museum. Added to the Swedish tree in Update 2.55 "Ninth Wave", it differs from the Soviet T-50 in that add-on plating on the hull front and turret, which together with the sloped armour helps deflect many hits. A 45 mm gun and two DT machine guns give it adequate firepower.
sw_t_54_1951: Finland received 43 T-54s and 73 T-55s from the Soviet Union between 1959 and 1972 and later modernised them, and some turrets even ended up as coastal guns. This version arrived with the "Fire and Ice" update and suits close-range brawling: the frontal armour reliably stops conventional rounds, though HEAT goes through easily and the cramped interior means a single APHE hit can finish it. The 100 mm D-10T has a strong APDS round plus an APHE shell best saved for flank shots, while mobility is only middling.
sw_t_55m: Between 1962 and 1972 Finland took delivery of 138 Soviet T-55As and 10 T-55Ks, and between 1989 and 1993 upgraded them to its own T-55M standard with a new fire-control system, laser rangefinder and Bofors smoke launchers; the type still serves as a trainer. It entered the Swedish tree in Update 2.23 "Apex Predators". Its armour is weak and it reverses slowly, but a capable APFSDS round, the rangefinder and a two-plane stabiliser make it an effective shooter.
sw_t_72m1: Finland's main battle tank from 1984 until the Leopard 2A4 took over in 2004 was this export T-72A with extra glacis plating, 162 of which came from the USSR and East Germany. It came to the Swedish tree's Finnish line with the "Fire and Ice" update and plays like other T-72s: a low silhouette that hides easily, an autoloader so there is no loader to lose, and strong forward mobility. The cramped crew compartment, the ammunition carousel under the turret and a very slow reverse punish over-extending, so it should not stray far from cover.
sw_t_80u: Sweden tested a T-80U against the T-72M1, M1A1, Leclerc and Leopard 2A4 in 1991-1994; it joined late, won praise for protection, ease of use and engine power but was faulted for poor visibility and night optics, and the Leopard 2A4 was chosen as the Strv 121. Added in the "Fire and Ice" update, it matches the Soviet T-80U's armour and mobility but lacks the 3BM46 APFSDS round. The same flaws carry over too: a carousel autoloader with exposed ammunition, and mobility that trails Western designs.
sw_tgdgb_m40_lv: The Luftvärnsterrängdragbil m/40 put a traversing Bofors L/60 cannon on the back of a Terrängdragbil m/40 cross-country truck; at least two were built in 1941, and neither fought. In the game, which it joined in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it offers a hard-hitting gun on a reasonably nimble truck that has very little protection.
sw_udes_33: Two UDES 33 prototypes were delivered in 1978, built on retired Ikv 103 chassis as protected, mobile carriers able to keep pace with tanks: one carried Rbs 55 anti-tank missiles and the other Rbs 70 SAMs. Trials went well, and a revised design led to the Pvrbv 551 and Lvrbv 701. In the game, added in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it is a missile carrier in the mould of the M113A1 TOW, with armour that even rifle-calibre fire can sometimes pierce. The Rbs 55 outranges most guns, suiting ambushes and long-range overwatch, but struggles with tanks like the T-55AMD-1 and its active protection.
sw_veak_40: Bofors built a single VEAK 40 on the Strv 103 chassis, delivered in 1964 as a next-generation SPAA; its guns and fire control were advanced for the time, but the cost was too high and funding went to the air force instead. In the game, since Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it fires two 40 mm Bofors L/70 autocannons at 300 rounds per minute each, slews them very quickly and has a search and tracking radar reaching 12 km, giving far better awareness than the M163 or Soviet ZSUs. Mobility is decent and protection weak.
sw_vickers_mk_e_37: Vickers designed the Mk.E in 1929 as a cheap, simple private-venture tank; the British Army did not adopt the tank versions, but it sold to China, India, Finland and Poland and inspired both the Polish 7TP and the Soviet T-26, though it was outclassed by the Second World War. Arriving with the "Fire and Ice" update, this Swedish-tree example is slow and lightly armed, yet its 37 mm fires a fast APHE shell with a little filler, with AP worth carrying for tougher targets. Ten degrees of depression and a high turret help it fight over crests, but a 3.6 km/h reverse makes escape hard.
sw_vickers_mk_e_45: When spare parts for its Vickers Mk.E tanks dried up, Finland rebuilt 26 of them with components from captured Soviet T-26s, swapping the 37 mm Bofors for a Soviet 45 mm gun and mantlet and the Maxim for a DT; nicknamed "Englantilainen", they fought until Finland left the war and stayed in service until at least 1959. In the Swedish tree since Update 2.21 "Fire and Ice", it hits harder than the Vickers Mk.E and has slightly better mobility and armour than the Soviet T-26, along with a larger crew.
sw_zsu_57_2: Finland ordered 12 ZSU-57-2s in 1960 to replace its L-62 Anti II vehicles, but their lack of night capability limited them; the ItPsV 90 eventually took over and the last left service in 2006. This version arrived with the "Fire and Ice" update, pairing two 57 mm guns with a heavily modified T-54 chassis that moves well but is barely armoured. The high-velocity guns are more of a threat to tanks than to aircraft, since they fire slowly over time and scatter their shots.
swift_f1: Supermarine's Swift was rushed into production as insurance in case the Hawker Hunter failed, and the F.1 entered RAF service in February 1954, only to be grounded by August after a string of accidents and replaced by the Hunter that year. In the game, since Update 1.91 "Night Vision", it previews the Hunters: good acceleration, top speed and energy retention suit boom-and-zoom attacks, and its 30 mm ADEN cannons can destroy a target in one pass. It handles poorly at high speed, and although the strong take-off flaps can serve as airbrakes, turning bleeds energy, so dogfights are best avoided.
swift_f7: After the F.1's troubles, the Swift gained afterburning engines, a stronger structure and a longer nose for radar and cameras, ending with the F.7, the only Swift armed with guided air-to-air missiles (Fireflash). Just 14 were built, used for training and missile trials rather than front-line service. Added in Update 1.91 "Night Vision", it accelerates harder than the F.1, and its beam-riding Fireflashes can catch opponents off guard, even head-on. It still turns poorly, so careful speed management is needed to line up shots and evade the IR missiles common at this level.
swordfish_mk1: The Swordfish, nicknamed the "Stringbag", first flew in 1934 as a torpedo bomber and spotter and was already dated when the Hurricane and Bf 109 appeared a year later; it is best remembered for the November 1940 Taranto raid, in which 21 Swordfish crippled three Italian battleships. Present since the open beta, it is slow and hard to keep alive, which makes it a challenge some players relish. Torpedo runs should be flown low and fast, from straight ahead or behind the target, ideally about 1 km out, and bombs offer a fallback for ground attack.
swordfish_mk2: Introduced in 1943, the Swordfish Mk II gained a metal lower wing that let it carry rockets, and it spent much of its career escorting convoys across the Atlantic and Arctic, sinking several U-boats. It came to the game as a reward from the 2020 "Victory Day" event during Update 1.97 "Viking Fury". Low speed and excellent manoeuvrability make it a good aircraft for learning to hit ground targets, and eight underwing pylons take AP Mk I and RP-3 rockets as well as bombs.
t2: Japan's first home-grown supersonic jet came about because the subsonic Fuji T-1 could not prepare pilots for the F-104J and F-4EJ, and foreign options (the T-38, or a costly Jaguar licence) fell through; Mitsubishi won the T-X contract, the first T-2 flew on 20 July 1971, and 90 were built in early and late batches. Added in Update 1.87 "Locked On", it is quick and handles well for its tier and carries decent missiles, but it has no countermeasures at all, leaving it exposed to all-aspect missiles such as the AIM-9L and R-60M. Its strike derivative, the F-1, follows it in the tree.
t2_early: Representing an early prototype of Mitsubishi's T-2, Japan's first domestically designed supersonic jet, this premium performs identically to the tech-tree T-2. It went on sale with the "Fire and Ice" update but was withdrawn after the May 2023 sale, roughly six months later, one of the shortest runs for any premium pack; it has since returned briefly for Golden Eagles during the 2023 and 2024 T-2 first-flight anniversary events. It is fast and agile for its level with capable missiles, but without countermeasures it must pick fights carefully to survive all-aspect missiles like the AIM-9L and R-60M.
t_129_atak: Developed with AgustaWestland from 2007 for Turkey's ATAK programme, the T129 is an A129 Mangusta with stronger CTS 800 engines plus avionics and sights matched to Turkish weapons; deliveries began in 2014, and by 2024 Turkey had more than 50, with others exported to the Philippines and Nigeria. Added in the "Drone Age" update, it swaps the A129CBT's Hellfires for Turkish L-UMTAS and CIRIT missiles: the former are slow enough to be dodged, while the latter work well against lighter targets. Stingers, a strong 20 mm cannon and engines that get it into action quickly round it out, but it is fragile, so flares and chaff matter.
ta-152c: The Ta 152 C-3 takes the Fw 190 Dora concept about as far as it went, pairing a shorter, redesigned wing like that of the late Fw 190 D-13 with a Daimler-Benz DB 603 engine for mid-altitude fighting. In the game it should gain height and speed first and then boom-and-zoom, a method that suits attacks on heavy bombers such as the B-17. Four 20 mm MG 151s plus a hub-firing MK 103 hit hard, though ammunition needs rationing, and the strong, fast-deploying flaps allow a tight emergency turn at little energy cost. It came in Update 1.57 "Battle March".
ta-152h-1: Kurt Tank's Ta 152 H was the high-altitude member of a Fw 190 D-derived family built to meet Allied bombers, with longer wings, a stretched fuselage and a Jumo 213E using MW-50 and GM-1 boost plus a two-stage supercharger; it could reach 755 km/h and over 14,500 m, ranking among the fastest piston fighters of the war. In the game since the open beta, it excels through speed, energy retention in manoeuvres and an air spawn, and its boost systems and flap-assisted turning keep it competitive lower down. Armament is two wing-mounted 20 mm MG 151s and a 30 mm MK 108 through the hub.
ta_154a_1: Named after the wooden de Havilland Mosquito, the Ta 154 Moskito was a fast twin-engined night fighter backed by Erhard Milch over Heinkel's He 219; when the RAF bombed the factory making its glue, a substitute corroded the airframes and caused several crashes, and it was cancelled in September 1944 with about 50 built. It joined the game in Update 1.65 "Way of the Samurai" through the revenue-share programme. Heavy nose guns kill quickly, but it turns poorly at low speed, so energy tactics suit it; the flaps tear off above 450 km/h, while wings free of fuel tanks give it a roll rate close to the Fw 190's.
tandem_mai: Pyotr Grushin's Tandem-MAI was an experimental attack aircraft built at the Moscow Aviation Institute in 1938, with two wings set one behind the other to improve stability and give the rear guns wider arcs of fire. The unarmed prototype flew on 29 November 1938, but work stopped in July 1939 and it remained the only example. In the game, where it was a reward from the 2018 "Chronicles of World War II" event, the aircraft proves fast and nimble, carries plenty of ammunition and has well-placed defensive guns, but it bleeds energy in manoeuvres and its underwing weapons are weak.
tb_3_m17_32: Developed by TsAGI from the ANT-6 to replace the TB-1, the TB-3 was the world's first four-engined heavy bomber with cantilever wings, with variants ranging from paratroop transports to airborne carriers for small fighters. This rare premium has been in the game since the open beta. Its huge bomb load can level as many as five bombing points in an Air RB match and wrecks the thinly armoured tanks of its era, and survivability is above average, though its size and clumsiness make it an easy mark at low altitude. Given out in 2013, 2014 and 2022 events, it otherwise appears only occasionally in the Warbond shop.
tbd-1_1938: Among the most advanced torpedo bombers when introduced, the Devastator was soon outdated, and unreliable Mk 13 torpedoes undermined its record; of 41 committed at Midway only four returned, losses blamed largely on missing radios and poor communication. Added in Update 1.53 "Firestorm" as the first bomber in the American line, it can attack ships or land targets. Torpedoes must be released very low, under about 104 m or 250 m depending on type, and bombs are most accurate from low altitude. Its single forward gun can finish damaged targets, and it turns quickly enough to set up a second run.
tbf-1c: Grumman's TBF Avenger replaced the Devastator: a heavy single-engined torpedo bomber with a 1,700 hp Wright R-2600-8 and Sto-Wing folding wings, it served with the US Navy and Royal Navy and helped send a Japanese light carrier and battleship to the bottom around the Eastern Solomons and Guadalcanal. In the game since the open beta, the TBF-1C carries 2,000 lb AN-M66A2 bombs or Mk 13-6 torpedoes. Defence is thin, with one 12.7 mm dorsal turret and a 7.62 mm ventral gun, and the two forward 12.7 mm guns are underwhelming, so it is very vulnerable to fighters.
tempest_mk2: Developed alongside the Mk V, the Tempest Mk II used a Bristol Centaurus radial whose installation was modelled on a captured Fw 190; vibration, overheating and tropicalisation for the Far East delayed production, and none of the 452 built saw action before the war with Japan ended. In the game since Update 1.37, it is faster than the Mk V, but engine output falls away sharply above 4,000 m. Its turning is mediocre, so it suits boom-and-zoom attacks, using strong acceleration and dive speed to escape or rebuild energy.
tempest_mkv: Hawker's Typhoon successor had a new thin wing, a fuel tank ahead of the cockpit and a larger tail, and the Sabre-engined Mk V was built first because it was easiest to produce. Operational from April 1944, Tempests were soon turned against V-1 flying bombs, claiming 638 of the 1,846 destroyed by aircraft. In the game since the open beta, it is a pure speed fighter with excellent level and dive speed and decent acceleration; it can out-roll some opponents, but energy tactics are more dependable. Climb rate is unremarkable and the controls grow heavy above 650 km/h.
tempest_mkv_luftwaffe: This German-tree Tempest represents EJ709, which made a forced landing near Kerken in October 1944 after being hit by flak; repaired with parts from another wreck, it was test-flown by Luftwaffe pilot Hans Werner Lerche from January to mid-April 1945, and what became of it afterwards is unknown. Added in Update 1.43, it brings strong guns and a high top speed for a piston fighter, but a slow climb and modest power-to-weight hold it back. It also goes without the 150-octane fuel, which dulls its performance further.
tempest_mkv_vikkers: A single Tempest Mk V was converted late in the war into a tank-buster, its 20 mm wing guns replaced by two underwing pods holding 47 mm Vickers Class P guns with 38 rounds each; trials were promising, but the war's end helped stop any production. In the game since Update 1.37, it keeps most of the Tempest's speed despite the pods and still outpaces its peers. The high-velocity 47 mm rounds can pierce any tank at its level from above and most from the side, though the slow rate of fire makes them unreliable against aircraft.
thunderbolt_mk1: The RAF took 240 P-47s, using most as ground-attack aircraft in the Pacific theatre, where their range and payload won pilots' respect; they stayed in service even after Tempests arrived and were retired once the war ended. Introduced in Update 1.101 "Raining Fire", it is a high-speed fighter made for boom-and-zoom, with heavy firepower, good top speed, strong high-speed handling and a high structural speed limit. A large bomb and rocket load also makes it useful in mixed battles.
tiger_hac_france: The Tiger HAC was a dedicated anti-tank version of the Franco-German-Spanish Tiger, meant to carry TRIGAT missiles and Mistrals for self-defence, but it lost out to the more versatile HAD and never went into series production. In the game since Update 2.45 "Hornet's Sting", it is slower than rival helicopters but well protected, with about 80% of its armour made of carbon-fibre and Kevlar composites that can sometimes stop heavy machine-gun rounds. Infrared fire-and-forget TRIGAT-LR missiles let it shoot and duck back behind terrain, but unlike other Tigers it has no nose turret for air defence.
tiger_had_block2_france: Proposed in 2014, the Block 2 upgrade gave France's Tiger HAD new software, Rafael Spike-ER missiles and the ability to operate from ships, with all French Tigers due to reach the standard by 2025. Added in the "Kings of Battle" update, it differs from the regular HAD only in its Spike-ER missiles, which home on their own with infrared seekers. As with Germany's Tiger UHT, that allows quick strikes on armour while limiting exposure to SAMs. Stinger or Mistral missiles handle aircraft, and the nose-mounted 30 mm cannon serves as a last resort.
tiger_had_france: The Tiger HAD (Hélicoptère d'Appui Destruction) reworked the HAP for heavier support and anti-tank work, adding a stronger engine and newer weapons such as Hellfire II; developed with Spain in the early 2000s, it was to number 67 in French service by 2025, about 40 of them converted HAPs. Since Update 1.91 "Night Vision" it has given France a strong top-tier close air support option, thanks to missile approach warning, thermal optics and a flexible arsenal of Mistral or Stinger AAMs, HOT-3 ATGMs and Hellfire IIs. It can destroy targets from safe distances in both mixed battles and helicopter Enduring Confrontation.
tiger_had_spain: Spain joined the Tiger programme in 2003 and ordered 24 HAD-Es to its own specification, some built at Albacete; all were in service with BHELA I by 2018, and they have flown combat missions in Mali under Operation Barkhane. Placed in the German helicopter tree with Update 2.45 "Hornet's Sting", it differs from the French version in weapons and handling. Mistrals cover air defence, long-range tandem-warhead Hellfire IIs with laser and inertial guidance deal with armour, and Hydra rockets add ground-attack options. It has no radar, so spotting enemy aircraft takes extra care.
tiger_hap_france: Eurocopter's Tiger, given screen fame by a starring role in the 1995 Bond film "GoldenEye", came in several national versions; the French HAP (Hélicoptère d'Appui Protection) prioritised escort and light support over tank hunting, and in 2015 France chose to upgrade its HAPs to HAD standard. This premium arrived as a pack in Update 1.91 "Night Vision", left the store after the 8th Anniversary Sale and returned in the "Hot Tracks" update for Golden Eagles. Missile approach warning, thermal sights, Mistral or Stinger AAMs, HOT-3 ATGMs and SNEB rockets make it a capable all-round helicopter.
tiger_uht: Germany's multi-role support Tiger, the UHT (Unterstützungshubschrauber Tiger), entered service in 2005 after a Franco-German development begun in 1984, and has flown reconnaissance and fire support in Afghanistan and Mali. A mast-mounted sight and fire-and-forget PARS 3 LR missiles alongside HOT 3 set it apart from other Tigers. In the game since Update 1.91 "Night Vision", it can scout and launch from behind cover with little exposure, but the PARS 3 missiles are slow, short-ranged and easily lose lock to obstacles or smoke, so targets may move off or be killed by others before impact. Timing launches and withdrawals carefully is essential.
tis_ma: One of the Polikarpov bureau's final projects, the TIS MA was a purpose-built heavy fighter rather than an adapted bomber like the Pe-3, though it shares the Pe-2's general layout of two underslung inline engines, a rear gunner and twin tail fins. It is smaller and slimmer than the Peshka family, and in the game it handles noticeably better and carries far more dangerous forward firepower, punishing anything that strays into its sights. It was introduced in Update 1.95 "Northern Wind" as part of the Operation F.R.O.S.T. event.
tornado_adv: Italy's Tornado ADV came from the tri-national Panavia swing-wing programme of the 1970s, in the air-defence version with better avionics and air-to-air missiles, and was acquired to replace the F-104S in front-line air defence. Added in the "La Royale" update, it carries AIM-9L Sidewinders, Skyflash SuperTEMP missiles and a 27 mm Mauser BK27. It outranges most opponents but turns poorly up close and loses energy fast in prolonged fights, so it is best flown defensively, keeping the initiative. It suits air modes far better than ground battles.
tornado_f3: The Tornado F.3 was the air-defence Tornado, first flying in November 1985 and serving with the RAF, Italy and Saudi Arabia from 1986; its Foxhunter radar could detect aircraft at up to 185 km, and the RAF retired it in 2010 in favour of the Eurofighter Typhoon. Introduced in Update 2.25 "Sky Guardians" in pure interceptor fit, it carries AIM-9Ls for close fights and SARH Skyflash SuperTEMPs, similar to the AIM-7M, for medium range. Track-while-scan radar, plentiful countermeasures and a radar-linked gunsight for its 27 mm BK27 help, but it turns poorly and drinks fuel, for which two 1,500-litre drop tanks are available.
tornado_f3_late: By 1996 the F.3 lagged well behind contemporaries such as the F-22 and Su-27M, and the Capability Sustainment Programme set out to add AIM-120 AMRAAM and AIM-9M; inconsistent earlier Foxhunter upgrades meant the fleet could not use the AMRAAM's datalink properly until the AMRAAM Optimisation Programme after 2003. Arriving in the "Seek & Destroy" update, the F.3 Late builds on the earlier F.3 with an improved radar and avionics, active-radar AIM-120s that engage from far safer ranges than Skyflash, and radar-slaved AIM-9Ms for close threats ahead of it.
tornado_gr1: The GR.1 was Britain's version of the Tornado IDS, the two-seat Panavia 200 design produced by a British, German and Italian consortium after the earlier AFVG and MRA collaborations unravelled; the first prototype flew in August 1974, and deliveries began in 1980 once engine, software and thrust-reverser problems were resolved. Added in Update 2.23 "Apex Predators", it stands out among Tornados for its TV-guided bombs, on top of the large bomb load typical of the family. It burns fuel quickly, though, and fights poorly in the air.
tornado_gr4: From 1996 the RAF upgraded all 142 of its GR.1s to GR.4 standard, adding night and all-weather capability, a FLIR in place of one cannon, defensive pods and precision weapons such as Paveway and Brimstone; the type flew over Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria and Libya before retiring in March 2019. Added in Update 2.41 "Firebirds", it greatly broadens the GR.1's arsenal with a LITENING pod, laser-guided bombs, infrared-guided PGM 500/1000 bombs and Brimstone, a longer-ranged Hellfire equivalent. The engines give strong afterburning thrust, but the aircraft is heavy and too sluggish for dogfighting.
tornado_ids_de_assta1: Germany's ASSTA1 package, finalised in 2000, rebuilt the Tornado IDS avionics with new fire control, GPS and laser-INS navigation and a 1760 data bus so it could use modern NATO stores such as the AGM-88 HARM, LITENING pod and Paveway III bombs; ASSTA2 and ASSTA3 followed. In the game, added in the "Apex Predators" update, this strike Tornado is nearly helpless against fighters in air-to-air combat. Its value lies in mixed battles, where strong ordnance and avionics make it an effective close air support platform near the top of the German tree.
tornado_ids_de_assta3_sle: Germany's Tornados went through successive ASSTA avionics and weapons upgrades, from ASSTA1 to ASSTA3.1, before the Service Life Enhancement programme launched in 2021 to overhaul each airframe, improve defensive systems and integrate modern weapons. Added in Update 2.51 "Spearhead", the SLE greatly widens the arsenal over earlier versions with a LITENING III pod, laser-guided Brimstone missiles and infrared-guided HOSBO bombs, along with countermeasure pods. It is still a heavy strike aircraft, though, and cannot contend with dedicated fighters in the air.
tornado_ids_de_mfg: Germany's navy received 112 Tornado IDS for anti-ship and maritime reconnaissance work; these Marineflieger aircraft, usually in sea-grey paint, could carry the AS.34 Kormoran missile and cluster munitions. Half moved to the Luftwaffe after the Cold War, and the rest followed when the naval units disbanded in 2005. Given as a reward in the 2022 Winter Quest during the "Apex Predators" update, it lacks the ASSTA1 upgrades and so has no guided bombs or modern targeting pods, but its radar-guided Kormorans are unusual. Weak in air combat and limited against tanks, it is mainly a collector's piece, with a niche against AI ships in Air Simulator.
tornado_ids_de_wtd61: Wehrtechnische Dienststelle 61 is the Bundeswehr's aircraft test centre, and its small group of Tornado IDS trialled the avionics and weapons that later went into the ASSTA standard, along with experimental kit such as a laser-guided Sidewinder. This premium pack arrived in the "Air Superiority" update and is essentially the Marineflieger Tornado without Kormoran missiles. Lacking guided weapons, it is outclassed in air battles and only middling at close air support, so it works best as a fast front-line bomber for earning Silver Lions and research with its premium bonuses. With just two AIM-9Ls and heavy, sluggish handling, it should avoid fighters.
tornado_ids_it: Italy's first Tornado IDS prototype flew in Turin on 5 December 1975, and by the early 1980s the type had replaced the G.91 as the core of Italian strike aviation, later flying in the 1991 Gulf War and over the Balkans; around 760 IDS were built in all. Added in Update 2.39 "Dance of Dragons", it is practically the German WTD61 Tornado minus its distinctive camouflage. High top speed, a large load of 1,000 lb Mk 83 bombs, decent guns and a ballistic computer are its strengths, while heavy weight, quick energy loss in turns, no guided weapons, a mediocre RWR and weak air-to-air missiles hold it back.
tornado_ids_it_mod95: This Italian Tornado IDS represents the two-seat, swing-wing strike version that Germany, Britain and Italy built together for low-level attack with precision weapons. Added in the "Apex Predators" update, it differs from other nations' Tornados mainly in paint, markings and targeting pod. A broad choice of guided and unguided bombs makes it an effective close air support aircraft, but it is weak in air-to-air combat.
tornado_ids_it_ret8: Italy's Tornado Mid-Life Upgrade, run by Alenia from 2003 to keep the fleet viable until its planned replacement around 2025, ended with the RET8 "MLU Full" phase of 2010-2012, applied to 10 IDS and 15 ECR aircraft with new electronics, a new RWR and GBU-39 capability. Added in the "Hornet's Sting" update, it greatly expands on the Tornado IDS (1995) with Paveway laser-guided bombs, JDAMs, GBU-39 glide bombs and a LITENING III pod. Air-to-air weapons and countermeasures are unchanged, and its poor manoeuvrability makes dogfights a bad idea.
tu-1: Tupolev developed the Tu-1 from the Tu-2 as a radar-equipped heavy fighter for interception, escort and ground attack, armed with two 45 mm NS-45s in the forward bomb bay and two 23 mm NS-23s in the wings; it tested successfully in 1947, but jets were taking over and the project was dropped. Added in the "Direct Hit" update, it is fast and heavily armed, though the 45 mm guns lack the accuracy and rate of fire for air combat. Three 1,000 kg bombs can each clear a capture point, two 450 mm torpedoes threaten destroyers and light cruisers, and mediocre acceleration means dogfights should be avoided.
tu-2: When Omsk switched to Yak-9 production in 1942, Tupolev moved to Moscow Plant No. 23, where the refined Tu-2S with uprated M-82FN engines and no dive brakes was developed in 1943; the seventh series of 1944 introduced a revised ignition system, and 1,776 were built there by 1949. In the game since the open beta, the Tu-2S (7) carries a heavy bomb load and strong forward and defensive guns, enough to down bombers and fighters. Self-sealing tanks and crew armour improve survivability, but a modest top speed lets interceptors catch it and it climbs slowly.
tu-2_early: Tupolev's "103" dive-bomber prototype flew in January 1941, and the production Tu-2 that followed used air-cooled M-82 engines because the planned M-120TK-2 was not ready; only 80 were built at Omsk in 1942 before the plant switched to Yak-9s. In the game since the open beta, it flies well for a twin-engined bomber, with adequate agility, a modest climb, and enough speed and a high enough speed limit to escape fighters. Three heavy machine guns cover the rear, the forward guns are useful at times, and it handles well even with a full bomb load.
tu-2_postwar: After the war the USSR needed to replace its Pe-2s, so Omsk Plant No. 166 restarted Tu-2 production, with changes including redesigned wing fuel tanks; 221 were built there between 1946 and 1949. Added in Update 1.29, the Tu-2S (1) offers a big bomb load and forward and defensive guns strong enough to shoot down bombers and fighters, while protected tanks and crew armour give it decent survivability. Its top speed is unremarkable against likely opponents and it climbs slowly.
tu-2_postwar_china: China's air force received Tu-2S bombers in 1950, using them against UN Command targets in Korea, in the capture of Nationalist-held islands off Zhejiang and against insurgents in the south-west, until new aircraft replaced them in 1977. Introduced with the Chinese air tree in Update 1.91 "Night Vision", it largely matches the Soviet Tu-2S (1), carrying a heavy bomb load for a front-line bomber along with forward 20 mm cannons and 12.7 mm defensive guns. It is not a dogfighter, but used carefully against unwary aircraft or unprotected ground targets it can change the course of a match.
tu-2_postwar_late: Irkutsk Plant No. 39 was ordered to build Tu-2s in 1946, but a fire delayed production to 1947; from the sixth series its aircraft gained a VEU-1 turret with a B-20E cannon for the upper rear gunner, and the eighth series a GSN-3000 generator to power it, with 218 built by 1950. Added in Update 1.29, the Tu-2S (8) is a versatile attacker whose moderate payload suits ground units better than bases. Its defining change is that 20 mm defensive cannon in place of the earlier models' 12.7 mm gun; otherwise it is much like the other Tu-2S variants.
tu-2_postwar_late_hungary: Late Irkutsk-built Tu-2s largely went to Soviet allies, and Hungary received 59 in 1953 for its attack and bomber regiments; during the 1956 uprising their commanders kept the crews in barracks, and IL-28 jets replaced them from 1957. Placed in the Italian tree in Update 2.35 "Alpha Strike", it differs from the Soviet Tu-2S (8) only in its Hungarian camouflage. A large bomb load, capable guns, protected tanks and crew armour make it effective and fairly durable, but it is not especially fast and climbs slowly.
tu_14t: Developed from Tupolev's rejected three-engined Project 73, the Tu-14 was reworked for maritime strike as the Tu-14T, gaining torpedo capability along with modern equipment such as ejection seats, a blind-landing system, IFF, a bombing radar and an autopilot-linked bombsight. Added in Update 1.65 "Way of the Samurai", the aircraft is close to the IL-28 in weapons and performance, with an airbrake as the main difference; it accelerates and turns slightly worse but tolerates almost 900 km/h before wing damage, so it can outdive an IL-28. Bombs up to 3,000 kg, a strong torpedo, a twin 23 mm tail turret and two pilot-fired 23 mm cannons complete it.
tu_4: After the US refused to supply B-29s, three American bombers that diverted to or crash-landed in the Soviet Far East were kept and reverse-engineered by Tupolev's team, with Soviet copies of the R-3350 engine and NS-23 cannon turrets; the Tu-4 first flew on 19 May 1947. In the game since Update 1.59 "Flaming Arrows", it is the Soviet tree's final piston bomber and outclasses the B-29 thanks to a larger load of heavier Soviet bombs, 23 mm turrets with more punch and range, and stronger engines. Jet fighters and early guided missiles are a serious danger, but an unchallenged Tu-4 can wipe out bases and drain enemy tickets.
tu_4_china: Ten Tu-4s were flown to China in 1953 as a gift for Mao Zedong's birthday; armed with American M2HB guns, they were used in the Tibetan Plateau campaigns, one became a gunship against ROCAF reconnaissance aircraft and another the KJ-1, Asia's first AEW&C aircraft, before the H-6 replaced them in 1988. Arriving with the Chinese air tree in Update 1.91 "Night Vision", it mirrors the Soviet Tu-4 except that its bombs carry far less explosive filler, offset by an option of eight 1,500 kg bombs. Strong defensive fire and high-altitude performance help, yet jets and early missiles can still stop it short of the target.
tu_95m: Tupolev's Tu-95 grew out of the piston-engined Tu-85, using NK-12 turboprops with coaxial propellers; the Tu-95M of 1957 added NK-12M engines, more fuel and a strengthened airframe, and 19 were built, with some older Tu-95s brought up to the same standard. It was a reward in the 2026 "Nuclear Thunder!" event. The main appeal is a very large bomb load, including heavy bombs, along with an RWR and countermeasures. It is slow and clumsy, so jet fighters and air defences find it an easy target, and its 23 mm defensive turrets struggle against fast attackers.
typhoon_mk1a: Hawker's Hurricane successor was accepted against Specification F.18/37, which called for twelve machine guns, but structural flaws could make it break up at top speed; development paused in 1940, then the Fw 190's arrival prompted a rushed introduction that cost several aircraft between 1941 and 1943, after which the Typhoon was reworked into a ground-attack aircraft. In the game since the open beta, the Mk Ia has outstanding top speed, climb and acceleration for its rank, ideal for boom-and-zoom. Its twelve rifle-calibre machine guns shred light aircraft but struggle against large or armoured targets.
typhoon_mk1b: A premium gift version of Hawker's Typhoon, the Mk Ib has been in the game since the open beta; it was withdrawn from sale following the 2017 Winter Sale and has returned periodically, both for Golden Eagles during RAF and D-Day mini-events from 2018 to 2024 and in sales such as the 2020 Battle of Britain anniversary. Compared with the Mk Ia, its big gain is firepower, with four 20 mm Hispano Mk II cannons plus heavier bombs and rockets, though it has slightly less engine power and flight performance than the Mk Ib/L.
typhoon_mk1b_late: In the game since the open beta, the Typhoon Mk Ib/L is a fast, heavily armed fighter-bomber made for boom-and-zoom. Four Hispano cannons with an air-targets belt destroy fighters quickly, and once fully upgraded it reaches nearly 700 km/h in level flight, climbs very well and turns well enough to dogfight some opponents. It can carry pairs of 250, 500 or 1,000 lb bombs or eight RP-3 rockets, which hurt its flight performance, so in ground battles it is worth leaving them behind when enemy aircraft are the bigger threat; the cannons alone can deal with light vehicles such as the Wirbelwind or PT-76.
ucav_mq_1_predator: General Atomics developed the Predator from the Gnat 750 in the mid-1990s as the RQ-1 reconnaissance drone; after Hellfire trials in 2001 it became the armed MQ-1, flying over Bosnia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya until the MQ-9 Reaper replaced it in 2018. Added in the "Drone Age" update, it cannot be researched but is available for 750 spawn points in high-tier ground battles to every nation except the USSR and China. Thermal optics make it valuable at night or when other air support is unavailable, but it is slow and lightly armed, so it should keep well clear of SPAA; once empty, it can still spot for the team.
ucav_orion: Kronstadt developed the Orion between 2011 and 2015, first flying it in 2016 as a reconnaissance and strike drone with 24-hour endurance and a 250 kg payload; it first saw combat in Syria in 2019, and around 48 are thought to exist. Added in the "Drone Age" update, it is Russia's non-researchable strike drone for high-tier ground battles at 750 spawn points, handy for players lacking a suitable aircraft or helicopter. It carries two supersonic Konkurs-M missiles: the tandem 9M133M-2 penetrates deeply but needs aiming at the turret or ammunition, while the high-explosive 9M133FM3 kills most tanks with a roof hit and destroys light vehicles easily.
ucav_wing_loong_i: Chengdu began work on the Wing Loong I after the Iraq War showed what armed drones could do, showing it publicly at Zhuhai in 2010; it has served with China's air force as the GJ-1 since the early 2010s and has been exported widely in Asia and the Middle East. Added in the "Drone Age" update, it is not researched but can be called in by Chinese players in ground battles for 750 spawn points. Its missiles can hit ground targets from long range, but the high cost means it is usually worth spawning only when no other close air support is available.
uh_1b: Bell's UH-1 Iroquois won a US Army competition in 1955 and was nicknamed the "Huey" after its original HU-1 designation; the UH-1B entered service in March 1961 with a slightly stronger engine and room for seven troops, and gunship versions with machine guns and rockets saw wide use in Vietnam. Introduced in Update 1.81 "The Valkyries", it is not fast but is very agile and can carry large numbers of rockets, six anti-tank missiles for engaging armour from a distance, or rapid-fire miniguns for hunting helicopters.
uh_1b_japan: Fuji Heavy Industries licence-built the UH-1B for Japan's Ground Self-Defence Force as the Hiyodori, with a domestic engine of equal power; it served mainly in disaster relief and carried rocket pods only for training. Added in the "Starfighters" update, it is armed solely with FFAR rockets, which leaves it exposed in combat. Like the AH-1G, it must fly cautiously and pick its moment to close in and unload its rockets on targets.
uh_1c: The UH-1C upgraded the UH-1B with a better engine and main rotor that cut vibration, improved handling and raised top speed; over 700 were built from 1966 onwards. Added in Update 1.81 "The Valkyries", it is set apart from the earlier model by BGM-71C ITOW anti-tank missiles. Otherwise it is the familiar Huey: slow but manoeuvrable.
uh_1c_xm_30: This premium version of the UH-1C carries XM140 30 mm cannons, a weapon no other vehicle in the game uses. It arrived as a pack in Update 1.81 "The Valkyries", left the store after the 2019 New Year Sale and returned briefly for Golden Eagles during the 2022 to 2024 "US Airborne Day" mini-events. It gives up the AGM-22 missiles, but since those are only the tech-tree UH-1C's starting weapons, its striking power hardly suffers, and otherwise it flies and fights much like the regular UH-1C.
uh_1d: Licence-built in West Germany, the UH-1D matched the American UH-1H standard with a Lycoming T53-L13 engine; 352 were made between February 1967 and 1981, and they served into the 2020s. Added in Update 1.83 "Masters of the Sea", it improves on earlier Hueys in almost every respect. Not especially fast but nimble, it can carry heavy rocket loads, six guided missiles to strike armour from a safe distance, or miniguns for helicopter hunting, though like its predecessors it has no armour or defensive systems at all.
uk_17_pdr_m10_achilles: Britain received about 1,650 M10 tank destroyers and from around 1943 rearmed roughly 1,000 with the 17-pounder to deal with Tigers and Panthers, making the Achilles the second most common 17-pounder carrier after the Sherman Firefly. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it hits hard once the Mk.8 APCBC is unlocked, though solid shot without explosive filler makes kills less certain, so aim for crew and modules, starting with the gunner on T-34s. Mobility is adequate, but armour is thin, the silhouette tall and the turret traverse very slow, so deep flanking is unwise.
uk_17_pdr_m10_achilles_norfolk_yeomanry: This premium Achilles wears the markings of the 65th Anti-Tank Regiment "Norfolk Yeomanry" of the 7th Armoured Division, and ranks among the earliest British tanks added to the game. It went on sale in Update 1.53 "Firestorm", was withdrawn after the 2017 Victory Day sale, and has since reappeared in the Warbond shop and in D-Day sales. Like the tech-tree version, it pairs an M10 hull with a 17-pounder whose Mk.8 APCBC punches through Panzer IIIs and IVs and can defeat a T-34's glacis, though damage is inconsistent. Armour is thin, the profile high and the hand-cranked turret slow, so close-range fights are best avoided.
uk_3_inch_gun_carrier: Built in 1941 as a stop-gap while the 17-pounder was unfinished, the Gun Carrier put an old 3-inch 20 cwt gun in a large fixed casemate on a Churchill chassis, since the breech was too big for a turret; about a hundred went to the 1st Canadian Armoured Brigade but never saw action before disbandment in March 1943. Among the first British ground vehicles, added in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it can hold a position almost alone with skill and support: the big gun wins frontal duels and Churchill armour shrugs off many hits, even from the side. Poor mobility and narrow gun traverse are the price.
uk_9a33bm2: The Soviet Osa-AK (9K33M2) improved on the original Osa and entered service in 1975; India received about 80 in the late 1980s, and at least 50 remain with the Indian Army as of 2025, due to be replaced by the home-grown Anant Shastra. Added to the British tree in Update 2.41 "Firebirds", it is functionally identical to the Soviet version, reliably engaging manoeuvring aircraft out to 10 km and guiding two missiles onto one target at once. Its wheeled chassis gives excellent mobility, but it is large, unarmoured and cannot depress its missiles far enough to fight ground targets.
uk_9a35_m: India took delivery of roughly 250 Strela-10M systems from the Soviet Union in the 1980s to bolster tactical air defence along its borders with Pakistan and China, and most remain in service. Added to the British tree in the "Storm Warning" update, it rides on the MT-LBU tracked chassis and carries eight infrared-guided missiles for short and medium range. The missiles fly well enough to catch manoeuvring targets, and a photo-contrast guidance mode allows lock-on from further out than IR alone.
uk_a17_mk_1_tetrarch: Vickers-Armstrongs began the Light Tank Mk VII, nicknamed "Purdah", as a private venture in 1937; it failed as a light cruiser but was built as a light tank, reaching units in November 1940, though engine cooling faults kept it out of North Africa. Many were sent abroad, including to the Soviet Union, and they served mainly in reconnaissance and airborne roles. Part of the original British tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is fast and well armed but thinly protected. Its 2-pounder penetrates most opponents up close, ideally aimed at the gunner first, but flat armour and a cramped interior mean one hit can finish it.
uk_a1e1_independent: The A1E1 Independent was an experimental multi-turreted tank begun in 1922, shaped by First World War thinking with many anti-infantry guns, thin armour and great length for crossing trenches; its single 1926 prototype influenced the T-28, T-35 and Neubaufahrzeug, returned as a static pillbox in the Second World War and survives at Bovington. Added in Update 1.63 "Desert Hunters", it benefits from a large crew but suffers from thin armour and a huge silhouette. It is surprisingly nimble for its size, if not fast, and its only shell is APHE with weak penetration but solid damage once through.
uk_a25_mk_8: Named after Harry Hopkins, the US adviser central to Lend-Lease, the Light Tank Mk VIII (A25) succeeded the Tetrarch with doubled, sloped frontal armour, but was already obsolete when production began in 1943; the order shrank from 1,000 to 100, all handed to the RAF for airfield defence, and some chassis became Alecto prototypes. Added in the "Hornet's Sting" update, it is effectively an up-armoured Tetrarch whose front shrugs off machine guns and small-calibre guns. The unchanged engine makes it slow for a light tank, but its small size still makes it a useful scout if not pushed too far.
uk_a27m_cromwell_1: Three designs carried the Cromwell name, but only the A27M with its Rolls-Royce Meteor engine reached series production; it fought from Normandy in June 1944, was used in Korea and by several other countries after the war, and led to the Comet, Challenger and Charioteer. One of the launch vehicles of the British ground tree (Update 1.55 "Royal Armour"), the Mk I carries the 6-pounder, which penetrates more than the Mk V's 75 mm, and it is slightly quicker because it lacks the later version's engine governor. In return it meets equally fast T-34s and nearly impervious tanks such as the KV-1E, with only adequate armour of its own.
uk_a27m_cromwell_5: Lacking a useful high-explosive shell, the Cromwell was rearmed with the 75 mm QF Mk V, a bored-out 6-pounder firing American Sherman ammunition, and in that form it fought from Normandy to Berlin and later in Korea; crews liked its speed but not its cramped interior or frequent breakdowns. Available since British ground forces launched in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it sits before the Mk I because its 75 mm penetrates less, and its shells do limited damage after penetrating. Its strength is outstanding forward speed, letting it reach firing positions first, strike and relocate much like an M18 Hellcat; accurate shooting matters.
uk_a27m_cromwell_5_rp3: In 1946 the Specialised Armour Development Establishment fitted a Cromwell V with four rails for RP-3 aircraft rockets along the turret sides, creating the one-off "Tulip"; it stayed a prototype, and a similar scheme was tried on the Sherman Firefly. Added in Update 1.59 "Flaming Arrows", it shares the Cromwell V's armour, speed and 75 mm gun, which works against Panzer IVs and similar tanks when flanking to weak spots. Because the rockets sit beside the turret rather than on a frame above it, as on the T34 Calliope, they can be aimed with the gun sight out to about 500 m, though judging their drop takes practice.
uk_a30_challenger: The A30 Challenger put the 17-pounder on a lengthened Cromwell chassis, needing a tall new turret for the gun and an extra loader at the cost of armour and mobility; built from March 1944, it fought alongside Cromwells and Shermans after Normandy, was generally preferred to the Firefly, and served Czechoslovakia until 1959. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", its gun, especially with APDS, can penetrate anything it meets, suiting sniping or flanking. It should not brawl: armour is poor, the profile large and reverse speed terrible, and apart from HE its rounds lack filler, so aim for crew and ammunition.
uk_a30_sp_avenger: The A30 SP Avenger tried to fix the Challenger's flaws with a much lower, open-topped turret on a lower superstructure, armoured covers for protection and return rollers to stop it shedding tracks; by the time the prototype was ready, priorities had shifted, it compared poorly with the Archer and Alecto when tested, and the project ended in 1950. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is a sniper and flanker: the 17-pounder and good gun depression make ridgelines deadly, and mobility is strong if a little below the Cromwell's. A poor reverse, slow turret traverse and weak armour make head-on fights a mistake.
uk_a30_sp_avenger_kit_3rank: The Avenger was a lighter, smaller self-propelled anti-tank gun derived from the A30 Challenger; it came too late for the war, with testing lasting into summer 1945, and 80 were built for two battalions before retirement in 1949. This version, added in Update 2.47 "Leviathans", is dressed as a typical late-war British tank with a camouflage net and a kettle hung on the back. It performs exactly like the tech-tree Avenger: nimble, with good gun elevation and a very powerful 17-pounder, but thinly armoured and slow both to reverse and to traverse, which makes it an ambush sniper rather than a city fighter.
uk_a39_tortoise: Conceived in 1943, like the American T28/T95, as an assault tank able to break fortifications such as the Siegfried Line while immune to return fire, the A39 Tortoise had 25 ordered in 1944, cut to six when the war ended. One trialled in Germany proved reliable, but at 81 tonnes it was very slow and hard to transport; the sole runner is at Bovington. In the game since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it lives up to its name: huge, slow and extremely well armoured, especially angled, with a 32-pounder that penetrates most opponents. Its sluggishness invites air attack, and the large commander's cupola is a weak spot.
uk_a_12_mk_2_matilda_2: Classed in the game as a heavy tank, the British Matilda III is, like the real vehicle, extremely slow but protected by formidable frontal armour. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it plays like a typical heavy tank, soaking up fire for teammates and hitting back while opponents struggle to get through. Keeping some distance from the front line makes its armour more effective, and its reputation tends to draw enemy attention.
uk_a_13_mk1: The A13 Mk I (Cruiser Mk III) was Britain's third cruiser design and introduced Christie suspension, giving more speed and better cross-country ability than earlier bogie-sprung cruisers, though like its peers it was lightly armed and unreliable. Most sent to France with the 1st Armoured Division were lost, and a few later served in Greece and Libya with the 7th Armoured Division. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is quick, agile and very thinly armoured, with a decent gun; it should scout, flank isolated targets and lay smoke rather than hold the front, and it can feel slow and slide in mud.
uk_a_13_mk1_3rd_rtr: This A13 Mk I carries the markings of the 3rd Royal Tank Regiment, which was diverted to Calais in 1940 and lost all its tanks in the four-day siege there, with many men killed or captured and some escaping via Dunkirk or by sea. Added in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour" as the prize in the 2015 Christmas giveaway, and at one time given free to new players who picked Britain first, it plays just like the standard A13 Mk I. Very fast and nimble with an acceptable gun and almost no armour, it suits scouting, smoke and flanking, and struggles in mud.
uk_a_13_mk2: The A13 Mk IIA (Cruiser Mk IVA) was the later-production A13 Mk II, with extra armour on the hull as well as the turret; 955 were built, serving in France in 1940 and early in the North African campaign, and it was among Britain's fastest tanks of that period. Added in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it improves slightly on the A13 Mk I's protection, though the armour still stops little beyond heavy machine-gun fire. The 2-pounder copes with most opponents at its rank, but lacks the penetration and accuracy for tougher targets at long range.
uk_a_13_mk2_1939: The first A13 Mk IIs (Cruiser Mk IV) were simply A13 Mk Is with extra turret armour, leaving the hull unchanged; only eight were made that way. This premium arrived in Update 1.53 "Firestorm", left the store in May 2016 and has since resurfaced in the 7th and 10th anniversary events, a 2017 April Fools sale, the Warbond shop and the Marketplace. The added 0.8 tonnes of turret armour costs no mobility but still stops very little, while the 2-pounder handles most opponents of its rank yet struggles with penetration and accuracy against tougher, distant targets.
uk_a_22_mk_1_churchill_1941: Britain's 1941 infantry tank, the Churchill I, combined thick armour with a 2-pounder in the turret and a 3-inch howitzer in the hull, though it was slow and mechanically troublesome; the type, named after John Churchill, fought in Operations Torch and Overlord and served until 1952. Added in Update 1.69 "Regia Aeronautica", its angled front stops most contemporaries, even the Panzer IV F2, leaving few tanks such as the M10 or Achilles able to beat it head-on. The 2-pounder is weak but reloads fast, the howitzer is best used for smoke, and quick neutral steering offsets slow turning on the move.
uk_a_22b_mk_3_churchill_1942: The Churchill III swapped the 2-pounder for a far more effective 6-pounder in a new boxy turret, replaced the hull howitzer with a machine gun and revised the engine and transmission; 675 were built in 1942. It gave the Churchill its combat debut at Dieppe and then fought in North Africa, including the Second Battle of El Alamein, while the Soviet Union received 301 Churchills of various marks. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it has thick frontal armour, a spread-out crew that helps it survive and a gun that handles most opponents. Low speed means it works best as a careful heavy tank.
uk_a_22f_mk_7_churchill_1944: The Churchill VII was the heavily armoured end point of the Churchill line, with 152 mm of frontal and 95 mm of side armour, strengthened suspension and the 75 mm OQF Mk V; it fought from Normandy to the end of the war, and roughly 1,400 A22F tanks (Mk VII and VIII) are thought to have been built. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is tough and survivable but moves slowly and has a fairly weak gun.
uk_a_22f_mk_7_churchill_crocodile: One of "Hobart's Funnies" built for D-Day after the lessons of Dieppe, the Crocodile was a field conversion of the Churchill VII whose flamethrower cleared German bunkers while its armour shrugged off small arms; unlike most flame tanks it kept its 75 mm gun, and some served in Korea until 1951. It was the reward for Battle Pass Season IX, "Smell of Victory", in the "Fire and Ice" update. It plays like the Churchill VII, with the hull MG replaced by a flamethrower that is lethal against open-topped vehicles but only briefly blinds enclosed ones, while the fuel trailer slows its reverse slightly.
uk_a_33_excelsior: Prompted by the early Churchill's unreliability and slowness, the A33 Excelsior was approved in 1942 as a universal tank based on the A27 Cromwell, but once the Churchill's problems were solved and Shermans had replaced the cruisers in 1943 it was cancelled. Awarded in the 2017 "War Thunder Chronicles" event during Update 1.67 "Assault", it unusually combines dependable armour, good mobility and a well-penetrating 75 mm OQF Mk V that has no APHE. Twelve degrees of gun depression, smoke launchers and solid angled protection help, but reversing is very slow and its large size makes it easy to spot.
uk_a_34_comet: Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", the Comet I carries the 77 mm HV, effectively a lower-velocity 17-pounder and one of the strongest guns on a medium tank at its level, especially once APDS is unlocked. It accelerates briskly to 38 km/h and holds that speed, though it reverses as poorly as the Cromwell. Armour is weak, so its low profile, mobility and good gun depression (an improvement over the Sherman Firefly before it) are best used to find hull-down positions and catch enemies at favourable angles.
uk_a_34_comet_iron_duke: Lieutenant-Colonel Pat Hobart, who led the 1st Royal Tank Regiment of the 7th Armoured Division, commanded from this Comet, Iron Duke IV. This version was a reward for the 2016 WW2 Chronicles event in Update 1.57 "Battle March" and plays just like the regular Comet I. Its 77 mm HV gun, a lower-velocity 17-pounder, hits hard, especially with APDS, and it reaches 38 km/h quickly, but reverse is sluggish and the armour is easily penetrated. Low height and good gun depression make hull-down positions and flanking angles its best tools.
uk_a_43_black_prince: An experimental Churchill VII derivative carrying a 17-pounder, the A43 Black Prince was conceived as a stop-gap "universal tank" before the Centurion; the bigger turret needed a wider hull, and the extra weight a revised suspension and wider tracks. The first of six prototypes appeared in May 1945, when faster 17-pounder tanks were already arriving, and one survives at Bovington. Among the first British tanks in the game, added in Update 1.53 "Firestorm", it reloads in 7.6 s and with APDS can kill Ferdinands and IS-2s beyond 1 km. Its armour is less dependable than earlier Churchills', and 17 km/h forward and 2 km/h reverse make it extremely slow.
uk_ac1_sentinel: Australia began developing its own tank in 1940 under threat of Japanese invasion; the Australian Cruiser Mk I "Sentinel" reached prototype stage in 1942 and 65 were built by June 1943, but technical problems kept it out of service and the programme ended as American M4 output grew. Its only "action" was standing in for German tanks in the 1944 film "Rats of Tobruk". Awarded in the 2021 Operation W.I.N.T.E.R. event during the "Winged Lions" update, it plays more like an infantry tank, with a thick, well-angled front and sturdy turret. The gun lacks penetration and damage but fires quickly, and acceleration is poor.
uk_ac4_thunderbolt: Australia's Sentinel line drew on the American M3 Medium, in the manner of the Canadian Ram, with some Crusader elements; planned with a 2-pounder and later a 6-pounder, it culminated in the A.C.IV with a 17-pounder and a 70-inch turret ring. Arriving a while after the British ground tree launched, it is a compact, well-rounded tank with a better armour layout than most British vehicles at its level, occasionally bouncing Tiger or Panther rounds. It reaches about 30 km/h quickly, reverses almost as fast as it drives forward, and the 17-pounder lets it trade blows with better-armoured opponents.
uk_adats_m113a3: Canada's ADATS (Air Defence Anti-Tank System) mounted eight dual-role missiles, a radar and fire-control equipment on an M113A2; they were stationed in West Germany under Canada's NATO commitment until 1994, and all 36 systems were retired in 2012. Added in the "Hot Tracks" update, it works as both tank destroyer and SPAA thanks to MIM-146 missiles with a warhead equal to 6 kg of TNT and up to 900 mm of penetration. Their 10 km reach against aircraft is sometimes too short, and unlike the American ADATS it has no cannon.
uk_ajax: General Dynamics UK based the Ajax on the ASCOD 2 to replace the ageing CVR(T) family, and 1,010 were ordered in 2014, but noise and vibration that left crews with nausea, swollen joints and tinnitus delayed service until January 2025, with further sickness reports that November; deliveries are due to finish around 2028-29. Added in the "Line of Contact" update, it is a flexible vehicle whose 40 mm cased-telescoped cannon penetrates well, and with optional IRST and high-resolution thermals it can engage aircraft as well as vehicles. Armour only stops autocannon fire, and the three crew sit close enough for one anti-tank round to knock them all out.
uk_alecto_mk_1: Built on the Harry Hopkins light tank chassis, the Alecto Mk I was an experimental light self-propelled gun whose development dragged on until a production-ready version appeared in June 1945, when better vehicles already existed; a small batch was built, used only for training and scrapped by 1955. A reward from the "Battle for Arachis" event in the "Wind of Change" update, it is a glass cannon: the 95 mm howitzer fires powerful HE and HEAT, but reloads slowly and the vehicle has almost no armour. Decent mobility and a tiny profile help, so it should fire from range and relocate often.
uk_arjun_mk1: India's Arjun programme began after the 1971 war to replace the Vijayanta, with Krauss-Maffei Wegmann assisting; prototypes came in 1984-87, testing ran from 1993 to 1996, and the tank entered service only in 2004, with 124 production vehicles delivered by 2011 against an original plan for 2,000. Added in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey", it is essentially a Leopard 2A4 that gives up turret blow-out panels in exchange for better ammunition and thermal sights. Its 120 mm MK-II FSAPDS round penetrates most opponents, the turret is well armoured and it reaches 70 km/h, but the hull is weak and a turret ammunition hit is usually fatal.
uk_armored_car_aec_mk_2: After meeting Italian armoured cars in North Africa, AEC designed its own while the Daimler was still in development; 629 entered service from 1941, and the Mk II brought a larger three-man turret with a 6-pounder, a reshaped nose and a 158 hp diesel. It was a reward from the 2017-18 "Festive Quest" during Update 1.75 "La Résistance". Essentially the AEC AA with a 57 mm 6-pounder turret in place of twin 20 mm Oerlikons, it sits lower and is easier to hide, and a 7.62 mm BESA helps against open-topped SPAA and SPGs.
uk_armored_car_mk_2_aa: AEC based its armoured car on the Matador artillery tractor in 1941, impressing Churchill at a parade; 629 were built in 1942-43 and fought in North Africa with 2-pounder, 6-pounder or 75 mm guns. In 1944 a prototype mounted the twin 20 mm Oerlikon turret of the Crusader AA Mk II, but Allied air superiority meant it was never mass-produced. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is an effective wheeled anti-aircraft vehicle that also threatens light armour, with armour that resists heavy machine guns and high road speed, though cross-country ability is mediocre.
uk_as_90_mk_2: When the multinational SP70 howitzer project ran into trouble, Britain developed its own system from 1982, and Vickers Shipbuilding and Engineering's design won in March 1985 as the AS90 (Artillery System for the 1990s), replacing the Abbot and M109 in five regiments. It served with NATO in Bosnia and Kosovo and in Iraq in 2003. Added in Update 2.55 "Ninth Wave", it carries a fast-loading 155 mm gun with HE shells for ground targets and proximity-fuzed HE for aircraft. Protection is light and the vehicle is big, so almost any direct hit can destroy it.
uk_badger: South Africa's Hoefyster programme set out in 2007 to replace the ageing Ratel with the Badger, a Patria-based wheeled IFV planned in several versions, but supplier Denel Land Systems lost the ability to deliver and the programme was suspended indefinitely in November 2024. Added in Update 2.47 "Leviathans", it carries a 30 mm cannon that cannot win frontal duels with most opponents, so it relies on flanking with its good acceleration and speed over any terrain. The front may stop 20 mm rounds, unreliably, while the sides fall to 12.7 mm fire, but a spread-out crew of four and rear fuel tanks and ammunition stowage aid survival.
uk_bosvark: During the Border War, South African forces captured enough Soviet ZU-23-2 guns from the MPLA to field them, and in the early 1990s mounted them, as the GA-6, on the SAMIL-100 Kwêvol armoured truck to fill the gap left by the retired Ystervark. Added in the "Fire and Ice" update, it is quick and nimble for its size, and a short burst from its 23 mm cannons can bring down an aircraft, so it suits ambushes from cover. It is large, many crew are exposed, the ammunition runs out quickly with a long reload, and it can neither fire forward nor penetrate most tanks.
uk_boxer_crv_block2: Australia's LAND 400 programme chose the Boxer CRV to replace its ASLAV, ordering 211 for delivery from 2021 to 2026; after 25 Block I vehicles, Rheinmetall is building the 186 Block II locally, with a two-man Lance turret, 30 mm cannon and Spike LR2 missiles. It was a reward from the 2025 Winter Concert event. In the game it is a fast wheeled IFV whose cannon has belts for light vehicles and aircraft plus several armour-piercing rounds, while the Spike missiles can hit tanks and helicopters from long range. Protection is average, helped by a side-mounted active protection system, but missile stowage is small and the vehicle is large.
uk_centurion_action_x: "Action X" is the nickname for the Centurion Mantletless Turret, a project to give the Centurion a steeply sloped turret without a gun mantlet, inspired by the Chieftain; it was not widely adopted, and one example survives at Bovington. Added in Update 1.93 "Shark Attack", it resembles the FV4202 but has a thicker if less sloped glacis, different turret contours and a stronger engine for slightly better mobility. Otherwise it plays like other 20-pounder Centurions, balancing mobility and firepower, with the sloped turret adding resilience in a British post-war line-up.
uk_centurion_mk_1: Begun in October 1943 to a War Office requirement for a 45-tonne tank with a 650 hp engine, sloped frontal armour and the 17-pounder, the Centurion arrived just as the war in Europe ended; Cold War and export demand then drove a long family of variants, and it is widely counted among the best tanks of the post-war era. Added in Update 1.67 "Assault", the Mk 1 combines solid armour, excellent mobility and the proven 17-pounder. It was also among the first British vehicles with an overhauled transmission giving a much better reverse, so it can fire and pull back into cover before the enemy responds.
uk_centurion_mk_10: Built by Vickers from 1959 and produced between 1960 and 1972, the Centurion Mk 10 carried the 105 mm L7A1, Britain's most successful tank gun, which also armed the Leopard 1 and, as the M68, American M48s and M60s; Mk 10s served with many armies and fought in Vietnam, the Middle East and the Iran-Iraq War. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it hits far harder than earlier Centurions, though ammunition is limited to APDS, with about 350 mm of penetration, and HESH. Armour is much like the Mk 3's, and the heavy hull with a modest engine leaves mobility below average.
uk_centurion_mk_2: Built to counter the Soviet tank threat, the Centurion Mk 2 added heavier armour, a fully cast turret and a two-plane stabiliser for the 17-pounder; 800 were ordered in November 1945, it joined the 5th Royal Tank Regiment in December 1946, and all were later rebuilt to Mk 3 standard or as recovery vehicles. This premium was the reward for Battle Pass Season XI, "Her Majesty's Hussar", in the "Sky Guardians" update. Its stabiliser, among the first in the game, keeps the sights steady while moving, so it can shoot on the move and play far more aggressively than the Mk 1.
uk_centurion_mk_3: Introduced in 1948, the Centurion Mk 3 brought the 84 mm 20-pounder, whose heavier rounds could defeat the front of the T-34-85 and IS-2 or IS-3, along with an improved two-plane stabiliser for firing on the move; a Besa machine gun replaced the planned 20 mm Polsten. It served widely in Korea, slightly outperforming the M26 and M46. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it plays much like a modern MBT: the stabilised gun lets it engage first while manoeuvring, and APDS with up to 384 mm of penetration lets it confront heavy tanks head-on.
uk_centurion_mk_3_ss11: Sweden's Strv 81 (RB 52) was a Centurion Mk 3 equipped with the RB 52, a local copy of Nord Aviation's SS.11 wire-guided MCLOS missile. This version arrived in the British tree in Update 1.59 "Flaming Arrows" and left the store after the 2020 May sale, with an identical copy later placed in the Swedish tree. It handles like a stabilised Centurion Mk 3, plus three ready RB 52s on the turret's right side that penetrate up to 600 mm. Because the missile climbs before settling onto its path, it cannot properly hit anything within about 200 m, so engagement range needs watching.
uk_centurion_mk_5_avre_era: The Centurion Mk.5 AVRE was an engineer vehicle for breaching minefields with a towed Giant Viper, demolishing fortifications with its 165 mm L9A1 gun firing 29 kg HESH, and clearing debris with a dozer blade; some were up-armoured for the 1991 Gulf War. Sold as a premium pack from Update 1.79 "Project X" until the 2023 New Year Sale, it is one of only two vehicles with the 165 mm gun, alongside the M728 CEV. ROMOR-A ERA on the turret and upper hull adds about 30 mm against kinetic rounds and 300 mm against HEAT, but its slow shell and poor mobility favour close urban maps.
uk_centurion_mk_5_raac: The Centurion Mk.5 of 1955 was a Mk.3 with extra machine guns and minor changes, and the Mk.5/1 added a plate to the lower glacis; 221 were produced, some converted from Australian tanks, and 58 served with Australia in Vietnam before Leopard 1s replaced them in the 1980s. It was the reward for Battle Pass Season II, "Steel Centurion", in the "Hot Tracks" update. Compared with the Mk 3, it gains that extra lower-glacis plate and a 12.7 mm coaxial machine gun, alongside good protection, a 20-pounder with AP and APDS, and a two-plane stabiliser. Its mobility is lacking, so it often trails its team.
uk_centurion_shot_kal_d: The final Sho't Kal variant, the Dalet, appeared in 1984 after the Lebanon War with the advanced "Barak Or" fire-control system and better-placed Blazer ERA; it served the IDF until Merkavas fully replaced it in 1992 and was used for training until 2002. Added to the British tree in Update 1.85 "Supersonic", it is close to the Israeli Sho't Kal Gimel but has excellent fire control for its level, including a thermal sight that sees through bushes. The 105 mm with HEATFS and APFSDS gives strong firepower and gun handling, while acceleration is mediocre and side armour only stops heavy machine guns.
uk_challenger_1: Vickers developed the Challenger 1 from the Shir 2 export design for Iran, keeping its 120 mm gun and adding Chobham armour, a Rolls-Royce engine and hydropneumatic suspension; the Mk.2, with gunner's IR equipment, followed in 1985-86, and Challenger 1s destroyed more than 300 Iraqi tanks in the Gulf War before British service ended in 2001. Added in Update 1.77 "Advancing Storm", it is best on the defensive, using its strong turret to fire from cover while hiding the weaker hull. First-generation thermals and a laser rangefinder help at range, but mobility is average, pivoting and turret traverse are slow, and the engine deck hampers firing to the rear.
