uk_challenger_1_mk_3_gulf: Challengers entered service in 1983 and proved themselves in Operation Granby, the British part of the Gulf War, destroying T-55s and Type 69s without loss; one made the longest recorded tank-on-tank kill, at 5.1 km in 1991. Added in the "Danger Zone" update, the Challenger Mk.3 Desert Storm matches the tech-tree Mk.3 apart from its appearance and the absence of ROMOR-A ERA at the front. It is heavy and slow to accelerate but reaches a good top speed, reverses very well, and its 120 mm gun with first-generation gunner's thermals gives it strong firepower.
uk_challenger_2_bn: The Black Night was BAE Systems' demonstrator for the Challenger 2 life extension project, shown in September 2018 with a Safran Paseo commander's sight, new thermal imagers for gunner and driver, a laser warning system and the Iron Fist hard-kill active protection system; Rheinmetall's rival proposal won instead, leading to the Challenger 3. Added in the "Wind of Change" update, it is a Challenger 2 built to defeat anti-tank missiles, with Iron Fist stopping ATGMs from both vehicles and helicopters. The APS can only intercept so much, though, so it should still avoid lingering in the open.
uk_challenger_2_dorchester: Dorchester Level 2F was an urban armour package for the Challenger 2, first used in Iraq in 2004 against RPGs, adding extra Chobham composite, ROMOR-A ERA on a frame at the front, side composite panels on hull and turret, and slat armour at the rear. Added in the "Starfighters" update, it shrugs off small HEAT warheads and some low-penetration ATGMs far better than the standard Challenger 2, though the kit is meant for portable weapons rather than modern tank rounds or heavy missiles. The extra weight makes it noticeably slower than the regular tank, so open ground and fast flankers are real dangers.
uk_challenger_2_lep: The Challenger 3 TD is Rheinmetall's entry in the Challenger 2 upgrade programme, the counterpart to BAE's Black Night, and was added in the "Air Superiority" update as the final tank of the British ground tree. It brings the Challenger line NATO-standard ammunition, improved ammunition storage and a proper commander's sight among other changes, pairing British and German engineering.
uk_challenger_2_megatron: The Challenger 2 OES was developed from the near-identical TES in response to the IEDs and urban fighting seen in Iraq, adding ERA and composite screens on the front and sides against RPGs and ATGMs plus IED protection, much like the American TUSK kit for the Abrams. Added in the "Air Superiority" update, it plays like other Challenger 2s, with the extra armour improving protection against APFSDS and missiles on key areas, especially the sides. The engine is unchanged, so mobility suffers further, and the lower front plate remains a weak spot best kept hidden.
uk_challenger_2_megatron_sm: This Challenger 2 OES is styled after the character Emily for the 2026 Senrai Maidens event and is otherwise identical to the other premium OES. The OES (Operational Entry Standard) traces back to the 2004 Dorchester 2F armour and a 2008 upgrade with Rafael reactive armour, and its "Megatron" test vehicle, shown publicly in 2013, trials equipment for the whole Challenger 2 fleet. In the game its extra armour packages help against ATGMs, but the weight of around 74 tonnes worsens the Challenger 2's already weak mobility.
uk_challenger_2_tes: The Challenger 2 Theatre Entry Standard, comparable to the Abrams TUSK, combines reactive, composite and slat armour in modular packages against tandem warheads and IEDs, along with a mobile camouflage system to reduce its heat signature and counter-IED jammers on the turret; the "Megatron" demonstrator appeared in 2013 and a revised version in 2016. Added in the "Winged Lions" update, it offers some of the best protection of any Challenger 2. The prominent jammer array on the roof gives its position away, making stealthy flanking difficult, and the unchanged engine leaves it slower to accelerate and turn than the standard tank.
uk_challenger_2e: The Challenger 2E was an export version with SAGEM panoramic day/thermal sights for commander and gunner, hunter-killer capability and a 1,500 hp EuroPowerPack built around a transverse MTU MT883 diesel and Renk transmission; offered mainly to Greece, it lost to the Leopard 2, and marketing ended in 2005. Added in the "Sky Guardians" update, it is very close to the standard Challenger 2 but with the much-needed extra mobility of the MTU engine in place of the underpowered Perkins CV12. That lets it reach key positions early and play a little more aggressively.
uk_challenger_II: Vickers began the Challenger 2 privately in 1986 as a thorough redesign of the Challenger 1, sharing only about 3% of its parts; in service since 1994, it has second-generation Chobham armour, a rebuilt turret and the 120 mm L30A1, hand-loaded by a four-man crew. Added in Update 1.87 "Locked On", it combines strong firepower and armour, but like most British MBTs it is slow compared with foreign rivals, so it often arrives at key positions late. The driver's hatch can be penetrated by almost anything at its level, so hull-down positions are essential.
uk_challenger_II_yt_cup_2019: Vickers proposed the Challenger 2 as soon as new requirements emerged after the Challenger 1, and it held its own against the Leopard 2, Leclerc and M1 Abrams in testing; delivered from 1994, it has served from the Balkans to Iraq, and Oman is its only other operator. This version was the grand prize of the 2019 YouTube Cup in Update 1.89 "Imperial Navy". It has a powerful gun but no HEAT, making lightly armoured targets awkward, and it is heavy and loses speed in turns, though it tops 60 km/h and reverses at 38 km/h. The turret is well protected, but the lower front plate lacks composite armour.
uk_challenger_mk_3: The Challenger Mk.3 is a British main battle tank added in Update 1.85 "Supersonic". It keeps most traits of the Challenger Mk.2, including its accurate gun and 1,200 hp engine, but adds ROMOR-A ERA over the lower glacis and sides and armour plating around the ammunition stowage. The extra weight trims its mobility and acceleration slightly.
uk_charioteer_mk_7: To make use of surplus Cromwells as Centurion production began and Soviet aggression was feared, Britain fitted them with a 20-pounder in a larger but thinner-skinned two-man turret; 442 were converted in 1951-52, mostly from Mk VII hulls with reinforced suspension and wider tracks, and most were soon sold abroad, seeing combat in Lebanon and service in Finland. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is a glass cannon: the 20-pounder, especially with APDS, handles any opponent, and it is quick and agile. With only three crew and thin armour, one hit usually kills it, and an extremely slow reverse means turning around to retreat.
uk_chieftain_900: Royal Ordnance's Chieftain 900 tried to fix the Chieftain's weaknesses with Chobham armour, a 900 hp Rolls-Royce Condor diesel and new suspension, transmission and fire control; prototypes built on two undelivered Iranian hulls were shown in 1982, though with mock-up armour, and with no orders it was dropped in 1986. Added in the "Spearhead" update, it cures the Chieftain Mk 3 and Mk 5's poor mobility with much better acceleration and top speed, and adds a laser rangefinder and L23 APFSDS. The lower glacis is still vulnerable, and hull and turret protection remain inadequate.
uk_chieftain_marksman: GEC-Marconi's Marksman turret, with twin 35 mm Oerlikon guns and Gepard-like performance, was designed to fit obsolete tank hulls; a Chieftain-based prototype was tested, but the British Army declined it, and Finland became the only user with its ItPsV 90. Added in Update 1.79 "Project X" as Britain's first radar SPAA, it is slow because of its underpowered hull and less suited to tank hunting than its Finnish relative, though excellent gun depression helps it use terrain. Widely spaced guns and a big unarmoured turret are liabilities up close, but capable radar and fast-firing guns make it deadly to aircraft.
uk_chieftain_mk_10: By the mid-1980s the spread of APFSDS and HEAT rounds prompted Britain to revisit the Chieftain's armour for the first time, fitting the Stillbrew add-on package to the Mk 9 to create the Mk 10; kits went onto tanks in service and new builds alike, keeping the type in use until 1995. Added in Update 1.71 "New E.R.A.", this final form of the Chieftain has a Stillbrew turret front that markedly improves resistance to early APFSDS, shaped charges and ATGMs. The L23 APFSDS round penetrates most opponents almost anywhere, but mobility and hull protection remain limited for its level.
uk_chieftain_mk_3: The Chieftain Mk 3 arrived in Update 1.57 "Battle March" and opened the run of Chieftains at the top of the British tree, pairing heavily sloped armour with a powerful 120 mm gun. Like the Centurions before it, it has a strong turret but a weak lower front plate, and although its top speed is higher than theirs, its overall mobility is worse.
uk_chieftain_mk_5: Developed by Leyland Motors and built from 1965 to 1983, the Chieftain was among the strongest Western tanks of its era, with a semi-reclined driver's position to lower its height; 2,265 of all marks were made, and the 1971 Mk 5 standard brought passive night sights, an electronic ballistic computer and a 760 hp engine. Added in Update 1.69 "Regia Aeronautica", it is still sluggish despite the new engine, and its lower front plate can be penetrated by many tanks. It has no HEAT round, but the L15A3 APDS, at around 300 mm, penetrates everything it is likely to face.
uk_churchill_avre: After the 1942 Dieppe Raid exposed the need for a vehicle to breach fortifications, the Churchill became the first Armoured Vehicle Royal Engineers, carrying engineer stores and a spigot mortar, the "flying dustbin", that threw demolition charges; it excelled among the "Hobart's Funnies" in Normandy in June 1944. A reward from the 2024 Operation Overlord event in the "Alpha Strike" update, it plays like the Sturmtiger, firing an 18 kg Petard round that is slow, hard to aim and effective only within about 100 m. Thick armour helps it get close, but the reload is long and a loaded round can be set off even by machine-gun fire.
uk_churchill_na75: Churchill crews in North Africa wanted better high-explosive firepower than the 2- and 6-pounder could offer, so REME Captain Percy Morrell showed that the 75 mm M3 gun and M34 mantlet from scrapped Shermans could be fitted to the Churchill turret; some 200, mostly Mk IVs, were converted before June 1944 and fought in Italy, notably at the Gothic Line. Added in the "Sky Guardians" update, it is a sidegrade to the Churchill III: penetration is a little lower than the 6-pounder's, but post-penetration damage is far greater. The Sherman mantlet also thickens the turret front, while mobility is essentially unchanged.
uk_concept3_ngac: In 1976 South Africa sought a "New Generation Armoured Car" to replace the Eland 90, which struggled to support the heavier Ratel; three 8x8 prototypes, based on the Ratel, Eland and Alvis Saracen (Concept 3), all carried the 77 mm gun from retired Comets, but none passed 1979 mobility trials, and later work led to the Rooikat. Added in the "Red Skies" update, it is a balanced vehicle with a strong gun, decent reload and ample ammunition, quick on roads but less so off them. Excellent reverse speed and terrain help protect its light hull, but slow turret traverse and a rocking chassis make quick shots difficult.
uk_conqueror_mk_2: Britain's answer to the IS-3, the Conqueror carried a 120 mm gun developed alongside the American M103's to give the Centurion long-range anti-tank support; delays with the gun and turret spawned the Caernarvon and Conway stop-gaps, and it finally entered service in 1955 with units in West Germany until the Chieftain replaced it in 1966. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it breaks from earlier British designs by stressing firepower and armour. Its gun can defeat heavily armoured targets at long range, and the armour and stabiliser allow close fighting too, though modest mobility and a long reload hold it back.
uk_cruiser_ram_1: Unable to get enough tanks from Britain or the United States, and with Valentine production in Canada hampered by imported parts, Canada designed the Ram on the M3 chassis in 1941 with a cast upper hull and new turret; Montreal Locomotive Works built 50 Ram Is with 40 mm guns before the 57 mm Ram II took over, and the gun tanks never saw combat. Added to the British tree in Update 2.49 "Tusk Force", it has decent armour and a fast reload, but its 40 mm gun penetrates poorly and does little damage.
uk_crusader_aa_mk_1: The first anti-aircraft Crusader III replaced the 6-pounder with a 40 mm Bofors in an open-topped, power-operated turret; issued to light anti-aircraft regiments from the Normandy landings, it was withdrawn soon after D-Day as Allied air superiority left few targets. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it struggles against fast aircraft because the Bofors fires slowly and its shells are slow, though one hit often cripples a plane, so patience and concealment pay. Its AP rounds can also penetrate light and medium tanks from the front and some heavies from the side or rear, but low damage means several hits are needed.
uk_crusader_aa_mk_2: The second anti-aircraft Crusader III carried twin 20 mm Oerlikons in a small, well-armoured polygonal turret that offered poor visibility for spotting aircraft; with the Allies dominating the skies over north-west Europe, few were used against aircraft, though some, notably with the 1st Polish Armoured Division, engaged ground targets. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is a much better anti-aircraft vehicle than the Mk I thanks to a far higher rate of fire, at the cost of almost no ability to hurt armour. Its enclosed turret protects the crew from strafing machine guns, but cannon-armed aircraft can still punch through.
uk_crusader_aa_mk_2_kit_3rank: This Crusader AA Mk II represents "Skyraker", also called "The Princess", photographed in Normandy on 7 June 1944 with the 5th Royal Tank Regiment of the 7th Armoured Division "Desert Rats", a circled star painted on its turret roof to deter friendly air attack. Added in Update 2.47 "Leviathans", it matches the tech-tree Crusader AA Mk II apart from a camouflage net on the turret. Good mobility and decent armour set it apart from most SPAA, and its twin 20 mm cannons deal well with aircraft, but they lack the penetration to fight most armoured vehicles.
uk_crusader_mk_2: The A15 Crusader was one of Britain's main wartime cruiser families, with over 5,000 built and a major part in the North African victories; the Crusader I of 1941 was nimble but thinly armoured and lightly armed, and the Crusader II added armour while keeping the 2-pounder. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is a quick short-range fighter whose fast-firing 2-pounder suits cramped targets, helped by a basic vertical stabiliser and much better cross-country handling than the A13. With little armour, it should avoid open ground and use its low profile, good gun depression and small turret in hull-down positions.
uk_crusader_mk_2_the_saint: "The Saint" was a Crusader II of the 10th Royal Hussars, a cavalry regiment dating from 1715 that fought in Operation Crusader, at Alam el Halfa and at El Alamein, where it captured German deputy commander General Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma, before serving in Italy. Added in the "Regia Marina" update, it is identical to the standard Crusader II. The quick-firing 2-pounder, a basic vertical stabiliser and agile handling make it an enjoyable short-range tank, but with almost no armour it needs cover, hull-down spots and its good gun depression to survive.
uk_crusader_mk_3: Because the Cavalier was delayed, the Crusader III became the first British tank with the 6-pounder, at the cost of a three-man crew and the loss of the auxiliary turret; a Mk IV Liberty engine eased earlier reliability problems, production began in May 1942, and around 100 fought at the Second Battle of El Alamein. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is a light tank only in its armour, as the 6-pounder can defeat most opponents frontally. Its low profile makes it easy to hide behind cover, and it works well supporting the front line, flanking or scouting.
uk_daimler_mk_2: The success of the turretless Daimler Scout Car led to a larger turreted armoured car using the Tetrarch's turret and a rear steering position for emergencies; it became Britain's main reconnaissance vehicle in North Africa and the heaviest British armoured car of its time. Added in Update 1.71 "New E.R.A.", it carries a 2-pounder on a 4x4 chassis and is meant for mobile support rather than absorbing fire. It shoots poorly on the move and turns in wide arcs, but a good reverse speed can pull it out of trouble, and a coaxial BESA is handy against open-topped vehicles.
uk_desert_warrior: GKN developed the Desert Warrior in the 1990s for export to hot climates, fitting the FV510 Warrior hull with a two-man Delco turret carrying a 25 mm M242 Bushmaster and two TOW launchers, with room for seven troops; Kuwait bought 254 and has used them since 1995. Added in the "Seek & Destroy" update, it greatly improves on the FV510's firepower: the Bushmaster handles light vehicles and side shots on heavier ones, and TOW-2, tandem-warhead TOW-2A and top-attack TOW-2B missiles deal with armour. Overall it comes close to the M3A3 Bradley.
uk_eland_90_mk_7: South Africa developed the Eland 90 in 1962 as a local version of the Panhard AML-90 reconnaissance armoured car. Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, it is one of the more pleasant British light vehicles, combining a small, very mobile chassis with good firepower, a mix the British tree otherwise rarely offers outside vehicles like the Crusader III and AEC Mk II. Its armour is weak, so it relies on flanking, scouting and ambushes against heavier tanks.
uk_falcon: The Falcon, added in Update 1.57 "Battle March", is a British SPAA with a sloped, rounded turret at the rear of a light tank-like hull. Most anti-aircraft vehicles either shred aircraft with high rates of fire but struggle against armour, or penetrate tanks but lack the explosive filler to down planes easily; once its modifications are researched, the Falcon handles both roles well. Its unusual look also makes it easy to recognise on the battlefield.
uk_fv102_striker: The Striker, added in Update 1.71 "New E.R.A.", is largely an upgrade of the Swingfire, using the same slow Swingfire missiles to strike enemies behind cover rather than snipe at long range. Five launchers, thermal imaging and good mobility give it a faster rate of fire and more margin for error, making it very effective at stopping pushes. However, its guidance camera sits low, unlike the Swingfire's raised mount, so firing over uneven ground or from cover often means exposing the vehicle to aim, which demands patience.
uk_fv107_scimitar: Alvis developed the CVR(T) family in the late 1960s to replace the Saladin, with the FV101 Scorpion (76 mm) and FV107 Scimitar (30 mm) as its reconnaissance members; the Scimitar's first prototype appeared in 1971 and deliveries began in 1974, with about 600 built against over 3,000 Scorpions. Added in Update 2.41 "Firebirds", it is closest in role to the wheeled Fox: fast and small, but its tracks cope better with mud and towns. Armour is very thin, and its ammunition may not penetrate heavily armoured tanks.
uk_fv107_scimitar_mk2: Drawing on experience in Afghanistan, BAE Systems rebuilt 50 Scimitars from 2009 with a Cummins diesel, automatic transmission, better mine and ballistic protection, new seats and air conditioning, plus optional add-on and slat armour; the Mk.2 entered service in 2011 and deployed to Afghanistan that September. A reward from the 2026 "Scimitar Strike" event, it gains slat armour that offers modest protection against early ATGMs and HEAT. Weight rises to 13 tonnes, cutting top speed to 80 km/h, though a 235 hp engine and new gearbox compensate, while thin protection and the slow-firing 30 mm remain weaknesses.
uk_fv221_caernarvon: To speed up testing and training while the Conqueror's gun and turret were still unfinished, its new hull was fitted with the Centurion Mk 3's 20-pounder turret to create the FV221 Caernarvon; troop trials in Germany, Libya and the Middle East exposed chassis problems, and all were rebuilt with Conqueror turrets from 1955. Available since British ground forces arrived in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is a heavier early Centurion, sharing the same gun and handling with thicker armour and surprisingly adequate mobility. It suits long-range support, but its stabiliser and armour also make it capable in close urban fights.
uk_fv4004_conway: Conceived as a stop-gap answer to the IS-3 while the Conqueror was in development, the FV4004 Conway mounted a 120 mm L1 gun high on a Centurion Mk.3 hull to protect the turret ring from recoil, which restricted elevation and depression; it was cancelled soon after work began in 1951, and the only prototype is stored at Bovington. Added in Update 1.57 "Battle March", it is all about the gun: armour and mobility are mediocre, but the 120 mm L1A2's APDS round rivals modern MBT penetration and can defeat any opponent, making it a dedicated sniper and fire-support vehicle.
uk_fv4005: After the IS-3, Britain wanted a gun that could defeat 152 mm of armour at 60 degrees from 2 km, and the answer was a 183 mm HESH gun; as a stop-gap it went on a Centurion hull as the FV4005, whose Stage II had a light enclosed turret and an extra loader, before cancellation in 1957. Added in Update 1.67 "Assault", it is the ultimate glass cannon, carrying the game's largest conventional tank gun, and even glancing hits do heavy damage. A long reload, limited traverse, a sluggish chassis and a turret that .50 cal fire can pierce demand caution, though the dispersed crew often survives one hit.
uk_fv4202: As the forerunner of the Chieftain, the FV4202 combined that tank's heavily sloped armour with a Centurion chassis, and it was added in Update 1.63 "Desert Hunters". It previews the later British medium tanks well, pairing a well-sloped front with a hard-hitting, high-penetration gun, and it is fairly mobile for its weight, letting it keep pressure on the enemy. The turret armour and lower glacis are its weakest points, so they should be kept away from enemy guns.
uk_fv438_swingfire: Britain's first dedicated ATGM carrier, the Swingfire was added in Update 1.63 "Desert Hunters" and has no cannon, only a light machine gun and two separately reloaded launchers that fire upwards. Its slow, mouse-guided missiles can be swung around corners or over rocks, so it can attack from complete cover and reach enemies hiding behind obstacles, though only the most recent missile is under control and targets can see them coming. It is best used to hold hills, streets and chokepoints against pushes, or to support assaults from behind teammates or cover.
uk_fv510_isv: Developed from 1972 to replace the FV430 series, the FV510 Warrior reached service in 1987, and about 1,000 were made; it served in the Gulf, Iraq and Afghanistan and was exported to Kuwait, but in 2021 the Ministry of Defence dropped plans to upgrade it in favour of the Boxer. Added in Update 1.81 "The Valkyries", it can either scout and ambush or use its ATGMs to flank and take objectives, and a thermal imager helps find targets. The lack of a stabiliser, however, seriously limits its effectiveness.
uk_fv721_fox: Designed in 1965 to replace the Ferret and Saladin, the FV721 Fox entered British service in 1975; its mostly aluminium hull stopped only small arms and splinters, but it could exceed 100 km/h and be airlifted, and after leaving British service in 1993-94 it continues with Malawi and Nigeria. Added in Update 2.35 "Alpha Strike", it can be pierced even by 12.7 mm fire but, at 32 hp/t and 104 km/h, among the best flankers at its level. The unstabilised 30 mm RARDEN fires slowly, but its tracerless APHE hits hard from the side, while APDS helps frontally.
uk_g6_spg: Nicknamed the "Rhino", the G6 puts the G5 howitzer on a wheeled self-propelled chassis and joined the South African Army in 1988; Oman and the UAE also bought it, just over 100 exported in total, and it has fought in the South African Border War and in Yemen. Added in the "Danger Zone" update, it suits long-range support from early positions, firing one of the most powerful HE shells in the game, enough to kill most targets in one hit. Quick on roads but slow off them, it accelerates very poorly, turns wide and is easy to spot, and its armour barely stops heavy machine guns at 200 m.
uk_khalid: The Khalid (FV4030/2), a forerunner of the Challenger 1, grew from the Shir upgraded Chieftains ordered by Pahlavi Iran; after the 1979 revolution ended that deal, Britain sought buyers for the parts already made, and Jordan became the only customer. Added in the "Apex Predators" update, it is a modernised Chieftain Mk.5 with a 1,200 hp engine that gives better mobility than British-service Chieftains and the fire-control system of the later Mk.10. Protection is its weak point, as it has no composite armour.
uk_m109a1: The American M109 howitzer entered production and service in 1963 and saw combat in Vietnam by 1966, exposing early flaws; the 1973 M109A1 added a longer barrel, stronger suspension and better turret drives and became the US Army's standard SPG for decades. Britain bought 140 M109s, upgraded them to A1 and passed them on to Austria in 1994. Added to the British tree in Update 2.31 "Kings of Battle", it benefits from higher muzzle velocity that makes direct fire easier, but like most self-propelled artillery its armour stops only machine-gun fire and fragments.
uk_m1a1_aim_abrams: Australia replaced its ageing armour fleet with 59 M1A1 AIM (Abrams Integrated Management) tanks from the US, refurbished Abrams with extra sensors and communications for networked warfare, which entered service in 2007. Added to the British tree as a squadron vehicle in Update 2.57 "Heavy Cavalry", it matches the American M1A1 AIM apart from appearance, with improved armour and fire control over the basic M1A1. Its KE-W APFSDS penetrates less than the M829A1 but is still enough for most opponents it meets.
uk_m1a2_sep3_abrams: Australia ordered 75 M1A2 SEPv3 Abrams in January 2022, along with breaching, bridging and recovery vehicles, to replace the 59 M1A1 SAs bought in 2007; they serve with B Squadron, 3rd/4th Cavalry Regiment at the School of Armour in Puckapunyal. Added to the British tree in Update 2.57 "Heavy Cavalry", it stands out for stronger turret and hull armour that lets it play aggressively and absorb APFSDS hits. It also gains KE-W A2 APFSDS and a camouflage net modification, but at 69.8 tonnes its mobility suffers.
uk_m3_stuart: Short of tanks after the losses of 1940-41, Britain bought American designs under Lend-Lease, receiving 1,784 M3s as the Stuart I and 1,594 M3A1s as the Stuart III. Sent straight to North Africa, they proved fast, reliable and tough, and unlike the Crusader II they had HE rounds, though crews discarded the useless side machine guns and range was short; they later fought Japan, and some went to China. Added in the "Starfighters" update, it combines good armour, pleasant mobility and excellent penetration, but it is very tall for a light tank, pivots poorly and its crowded crew layout hurts survivability.
uk_m3a1_stuart: The British name for the Lend-Lease M3A1, the Stuart III fought in North Africa with the 4th and 7th Armoured Divisions, where crews added dust flaps and removed machine guns; when Stuarts were misused against German armour in November 1941, 130 of 165 were lost in under a week, and by 1942 the M3A1 was kept for reconnaissance. Added in the "Starfighters" update, it is fast with a decent gun and a stabiliser for accurate fire on the move at short and medium range. Over the Stuart I it gains a better-sloped welded turret without a cupola and the stronger M6 gun, but its armour only stops machine guns.
uk_m44: Britain received the American M44 in the mid-1950s under the Mutual Defense Assistance Program as a stop-gap mobile artillery piece, replacing the 155 mm howitzer on some with the British 105 mm L13 to share ammunition with other systems; they were withdrawn from the mid-1960s and returned to the US in 1968. Added in the "Storm Warning" update, it is compact and mobile with a powerful 155 mm gun firing M107 HE and M110 smoke shells. Thin armour and an open fighting compartment leave it vulnerable to tanks and aircraft, limited traverse often means turning the hull, and the slow reload favours long range.
uk_m4a5_ram_2: Canada's Ram II combined the M3 Medium chassis with a new turret carrying the British 6-pounder; the first prototype was finished in November 1941, but it never fought as a gun tank, being inferior to the M4 Sherman, and served only for training in Britain until mid-1944, with many chassis converted into flamethrowers, observation posts and personnel carriers. Added to the British tree in Update 2.41 "Firebirds", it improves on the Ram I with a 57 mm gun that fires quickly and penetrates well, though damage is often lacking. Everything else carries over, including decent armour and an engine smoke system.
uk_mark_v: Britain's First World War heavy tanks, begun by Winston Churchill's Landship Committee in 1915, first fought at Flers-Courcelette in September 1916; the Mark V of late 1917 improved on the Mark IV with new steering and transmission and a stronger engine, though poor ventilation still exposed crews to carbon monoxide. About 400 were built, serving late in the war and in the intervention in Russia. A reward from the 2025 "The Great War" event, it is slow and thinly armoured, but its size and seven-man crew help it survive, and the sponson-mounted 57 mm guns work well up close. Rear ammunition hits, HE and bombs are serious threats.
uk_marmon_herrington_mk_6_2pdr: Better known as the Marmon-Herrington, the SARC (South African Reconnaissance Car) was a wartime South African armoured car, and this 2-pounder Mk VI opens the South African sub-tree in British ground forces, added in the "Ixwa Strike" update. It pairs a 40 mm QF 2-pounder with several machine guns, scouting and smoke, and it moves quickly over most ground, a trait shared with later South African vehicles. The balance of speed and firepower makes it a capable early light vehicle for players who work with their team.
uk_marmon_herrington_mk_6_6pdr: Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, the 6-pounder SARC Mk VI fixes most of the 2-pounder version's shortcomings with almost no new drawbacks, keeping its speed while adding far more firepower, which should appeal to fans of the Cromwell I and Crusader III. The 57 mm QF gun can quickly and accurately knock out even the heaviest opponents at its level, such as the KV-1 family. Thin armour and a reduced crew mean one good turret hit can end it, so flanking and ambushes suit it far better than frontal fights.
uk_matilda_hedgehog: Australian troops struggling against Japanese jungle bunkers prompted a 1944 experiment mounting the naval Hedgehog anti-submarine spigot mortar on the proven Matilda II; testing dragged on, even considering the M3 Lee as a carrier instead, and the war ended before it was ready. It was the reward for Battle Pass Season I in the "New Power" update. The rear-mounted Hedgehog launcher is deadly against tanks when used well but is a situational weapon, so the tank is less versatile than other Matildas. It also gives up the smoke launchers, and the launcher forms a large, unprotected ammunition store at the rear.
uk_mk1_grant: This premium British Grant I was the reward for the 2016 Operation S.U.M.M.E.R. event in Update 1.61 "Road to Glory"; it matches the American-tree Grant I, which differs from the M3 Lee mainly in its redesigned turret. Recognisable by its tall hull and two guns, it can brawl, combining the agile turreted 37 mm with the hard-hitting 75 mm in the right-hand sponson, or support from the second line. The 75 mm's APCBC with HE filler does great damage, while the high-velocity 37 mm reaches further and is the only gun with full traverse; poor turret depression and the tall profile make very close targets awkward.
uk_olifant_mk_1a: The Olifant Mk.1A is an early South African development of the Centurion with more firepower and mobility for long-range operations in hot, dusty conditions, and it was added in the "Ixwa Strike" update. Its GT-3 gun, a variant of the Royal Ordnance L7, keeps it competitive with NATO tanks at its level. The armour, however, offers little against the HEAT and APFSDS common there, and with a sluggish turret and modest top speed it relies on range, uneven ground and accurate shooting.
uk_olifant_mk_2: South Africa's Olifant Mk.1B of the early 1990s added a 940 hp engine, extra turret armour, side skirts and redesigned running gear; the Mk.2 upgrade of 2004 raised power to 1,040 hp and added a thermal sight and stronger frontal armour, entering service in 2007 with about 20-26 tanks converted. Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, it has an excellent thermal sight and effective APFSDS, but its old chassis limits both protection and mobility.
uk_ram_90mm_aa: The QF 3.7 Ram is a premium British tank destroyer from the Operation F.R.O.S.T. event in Update 1.95 "Northern Wind", mounting a powerful 94 mm anti-aircraft gun on a heavily modified Ram chassis; it serves as the British counterpart to the German VFW. Highly mobile, with a hard-hitting gun, a good crew count and a fast reload, it is built for knocking out enemy armour.
uk_ratel_20: South Africa's Ratel of 1976 was the world's first wheeled IFV to enter service and pioneered mine-protected hulls, wheels suiting the region's open terrain and easing maintenance; the Ratel 20 was the base version with a 20 mm cannon and MILAN missiles. Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, it shares the Ratel 90's chassis but swaps the low-velocity 90 mm for the 20 mm autocannon and seven MILANs. Better gun depression lets it use terrain more aggressively and launch missiles from safer spots, but the cannon cannot take on medium tanks head-on, and the underpowered hull prefers gentle slopes.
uk_ratel_90: The Ratel 90 is a fire-support version of South Africa's Ratel IFV for mechanised battalions, fitted with the same turret as the Eland 90 Mk.7, and was added in the "Ixwa Strike" update. It is the fastest British vehicle at its rank, suited to scouting and opportunistic flanking shots. That speed comes from having almost no armour rather than a strong engine, so it should be played like the Charioteer, as a glass cannon that also scouts for the team.
uk_ratel_zt3: The Ratel ZT3A2 was the final major Ratel upgrade, an ATGM carrier following the ZT3A1 of 1987 and able to fire the newer Ingwe missile; it remains in South African service. Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, it is a reasonably mobile wheeled missile carrier with tandem-warhead ATGMs, but its armour stops only small-calibre bullets, so staying unseen is essential.
uk_rooikat_105_td: In 1990 Reumech OMC began an export upgrade of the Rooikat, fitting Denel's GT-7 105 mm (a local L7 variant) able to fire NATO ammunition, plus a new thermal imager; completed in 1994, the single prototype attracted neither the South African army, which was content with the standard car, nor foreign buyers. Added in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it builds on the Rooikat Mk.1D with a heavier gun and DM33 APFSDS that can defeat any opponent, while keeping excellent mobility on and off road. Good gun handling and a gunner's thermal sight let it snipe, flank or brawl.
uk_rooikat_76: South Africa's search for an Eland replacement produced new prototypes from Sandock-Austral with Thyssen-Henschel's help, and the rear-engined Class 2B, armed with a 76 mm gun derived from an OTO Melara naval cannon, was chosen with a focus on reconnaissance and anti-tank work; named Rooikat in 1987, it entered mass production in mid-1990. Added in Update 1.95 "Northern Wind", it is a fast, agile light tank for ambushes, flanking and quick relocation. Its APFSDS penetrates even heavy opponents, though post-penetration damage is modest, and a two-plane stabiliser and laser rangefinder make it a strong long-range sniper that can also fight closer in.
uk_rooikat_mttd: The Rooikat Medium Turret Technology Demonstrator tested an autoloader in a small remote turret, with the crew positions moved down into the hull, and carried a non-functional mock active protection launcher. Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, it improves on the Mk.1D with a 105 mm gun like the Rooikat 105, an autoloader that matches ace-crew reload speeds and DM33 APFSDS, while keeping the family's excellent mobility. The compact turret costs it smoke grenades and machine guns, which can be sorely missed.
uk_rooikat_za_35: ARMSCOR adapted the Rooikat for air defence in the early 1990s, fitting twin 35 mm guns derived from the Oerlikon and an EDR 110 radar on a mast that could rise 5 m; the project was cancelled after just a handful of prototypes. Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, it works more like the Falcon than the Chieftain Marksman, with closer-set guns and separate radars that keep scanning while tracking, improving anti-aircraft performance. Its real strength is ground attack: even without APDS the guns shred light vehicles, and the Rooikat's mobility makes flanking heavier tanks easy, though the raised radar should be switched off when sneaking up.
uk_sarc_mk4_a: South Africa developed the SARC, which the British called the Marmon-Herrington, from a 1938 order, assembling it from American, British and local parts; 5,746 were built in all and used by many armies, though never in combat by Britain, and the Mk IV, with a 2-pounder and Browning in its turret, was the most common, over 2,000 made in 1943-44. Added in the "La Royale" update, it is among the fastest vehicles at its rank and carries the familiar 2-pounder. Its wheels turn poorly and struggle off-road, and armour and survivability are weak.
uk_sherman_II: The Sherman II was Britain's name for the M4A1, and Britain received 17,181 Shermans in all, about a third of production, passing some to Polish and Czechoslovak exile units. Added in Update 1.65 "Way of the Samurai", it plays exactly like the American M4A1, apart from access to late-war APCR. Its rounded cast hull gives the front plate a varying slope, but the hull-side joints, the cast construction and the vision blocks are weak points, though it still resists smaller guns. The early M34 mantlet protects the turret front less than the later M34A1 but allows 2 degrees more gun depression.
uk_sherman_ic_firefly: Built on the M4 (Sherman I) hull rather than the M4A4, the Sherman IC Firefly had a shorter hull with tighter suspension spacing; this one represents "Trzyniec", from the Polish forces that used Fireflies in north-west Europe and Italy. One of the first British tanks in the game, it was a premium pack from Update 1.53 "Firestorm" until the 2018 Summer Sale and later returned for Golden Eagles. It plays like other 17-pounder Shermans: as mobile as any M4, best providing flanking or long-range fire while heavier tanks lead, since its thin armour means it must shoot first.
uk_sherman_vc_firefly: Fitting the 17-pounder into the M4A4's turret created the Sherman VC Firefly, an improvised stop-gap that entered production in early 1944 in time for Montgomery's 21st Army Group in Normandy, where it was the only British tank able to penetrate German armour reliably; 2,100 to 2,200 were built by 1945. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it shares other Shermans' easy mobility, so it is quick to flank or reposition. Its role is fire support, from the flanks or at range, while heavier tanks lead, because thin armour leaves it relying on shooting first.
uk_sherman_vc_firefly_kit_3rank: This Firefly represents the type's Normandy debut with the 21st Army Group in June 1944, when it was the only tank able to reliably penetrate Tigers and Panthers frontally at combat range; the Germans made it a priority target, so crews painted the underside of the barrel white to disguise its length. Part of the "Echoes of Overlord" pack in the "Leviathans" update, it carries camouflage netting and that painted barrel. It plays like other Fireflies, with typical Sherman mobility, and works best in support behind heavier tanks, as most opponents penetrate it easily.
uk_shir_2: In the 1970s Imperial Iran ordered upgraded Chieftains in stages, ending with the FV4030/3 Shir 2, effectively a new tank with Chobham armour in the hull and turret front; the 1979 revolution cancelled the order, but the design became the basis of the Challenger after the MBT-80 was dropped. A reward from the 2025 "Enter the Serpent" event, it resembles the Challenger Mk.2 but lacks a thermal sight, has slightly weaker gunner optics and starts with a feeble L15A5 APDS, so researching L23 APFSDS is essential. The Chobham resists most rounds, chemical ones especially, but the engine is underpowered and top speed low.
uk_skink_aa: Canada began adapting its locally built Grizzly (M4 Sherman) into a 20 mm anti-aircraft tank in March 1943, naming it the Skink in February 1944; with no Allied orders, only three prototypes were built, one of which went to Britain for evaluation and saw limited combat use. Added in the "Drone Age" update, it has an enclosed, well-armoured turret that shields the crew from strafing, and a Sherman hull that holds up against other tanks. Four 20 mm Polsten guns make hits on aircraft more likely than the Crusader AA's two, but 30-round magazines demand short bursts.
uk_sky_sabre_fcs: Sky Sabre uses MBDA's Common Anti-Air Modular Missile (CAMM), developed for the FLAADS programme to replace Rapier, with launchers, a Saab Giraffe radar and a Rafael fire-control centre linked by Link 16; it entered British Army service in December 2021. Added in Update 2.49 "Tusk Force", the system is split into a Target Acquisition and Designation Sight vehicle with a radar reaching 120 km and two separate missile launchers. The TADS vehicle is large, weakly protected and unarmed, and losing it disables the whole system, so concealing it is the priority.
uk_sky_sabre_launcher: Sky Sabre is the British Army's CAMM-based air-defence system, developed by MBDA under the FLAADS programme to succeed Rapier and in service since December 2021; the extended-range CAMM-ER followed in 2023 with Avio. In the game, added in Update 2.49 "Tusk Force", these launchers come with the TADS radar vehicle without separate research and are deployed through it. They fire highly manoeuvrable CAMM or CAMM-ER missiles with active radar homing, inertial guidance and datalink, reaching targets at long range. The launcher is large, poorly protected against fragments, useless against tanks and inoperable once the TADS is destroyed.
uk_sp_17_pdr_valentine: To make the heavy 17-pounder mobile, Britain mounted it on a modified Valentine chassis with a stronger engine and an open casemate, pointing the gun rearwards because it could not sit over the front without overloading it; the Archer served in Italy and north-west Europe, and crews preferred it to the Achilles for its shoot-and-scoot tactics. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it carries the same gun as the Firefly and A.C.IV, which kills or cripples most targets in one hit. The reload is only average, so it should withdraw to reload when threatened, and its gun traverses further than most casemate tank destroyers'.
uk_stormer_air_defence: Alvis proposed arming its Stormer with General Electric's Blazer turret, combining a 25 or 30 mm cannon, two Stinger launchers and a search radar; shown in 1984, it drew no orders at home or abroad, and the prototype's fate is unknown. Added in Update 2.39 "Dance of Dragons", it is a conventional gun-and-missile SPAA for shielding friendly armour from aircraft and helicopters, comparable to the LAV-AD with the same cannon and Stingers but less ammunition. Its search radar aids detection and its small chassis moves well anywhere, but armour stops only machine-gun fire.
uk_stormer_hvm: Designed for short-range air defence against attack helicopters such as the Mi-24, the Stormer HVM carries up to 12 Starstreak missiles, whose three-dart warheads defeat armour and countermeasures and reach low-flying targets out to 7 km; it entered service in 1997, deployed to Iraq, was bought by Oman and later supplied to Ukraine. Added in Update 1.89 "Imperial Navy", it can threaten any aircraft, but its 7 km reach is limited and fast, agile targets reduce its effectiveness. It is best spawned early to deal with helicopters quickly, and can also hit lightly armoured vehicles.
uk_t17e2: Ordered by US Army Ordnance in 1941 and shaped by British needs in North Africa, the T17 armoured car led to the T17E2, with a Frazer-Nash turret carrying two .50 cal M2 Brownings, and about 789 were converted between October 1943 and April 1944. Part of the original British ground tree in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it is a fast SPAA, excellent on roads and rock but poor in mud, sand and snow, with armour that stops many small shells. Its two 12.7 mm machine guns are light next to the 20 mm cannons of German and Japanese rivals, so it relies on rate of fire.
uk_t_90s_bheeshma: India bought 310 Russian-built T-90S tanks, assembled or as kits, in 2001, and the Heavy Vehicles Factory has produced a further 330 locally since 2006; named Bhishma after a Mahabharata hero, they carry a DRDO-developed mine plough. Added as a squadron vehicle in the "Sons of Attila" update, it is the export tank on which Russia's T-90A was based, with similar protection and the same mobility, and the plough can sometimes absorb incoming shells. Export limits restrict it to 3BM42 as its only APFSDS, but ATGMs, HE-FS and that dart cover most situations.
uk_tog_2: Designed in 1940 by "The Old Gang", First World War tank veterans expecting another trench war, the TOG II had a very long, narrow hull for crossing trenches and managed only 13.7 km/h against an expected 25; later fitted with the prototype Challenger turret and a 28-pounder, it was cancelled in 1943, and the sole example is at Bovington. The reward for the 11th anniversary "Dreams Come True" event in the "Kings of Battle" update, it weighs 81 tonnes with add-on armour yet is only moderately protected and very slow. Its 94 mm 28-pounder penetrates well and the turret traverses quickly, so it works best supporting from behind allies.
uk_tracked_rapier: The towed Rapier SAM entered service in 1971 but its immobility left it exposed, so BAC put the launcher and a new radar onto an American M548 tracked carrier, showing it at the 1977 Paris Air Show; the Royal Artillery received it from 1983, used it in the Gulf War and replaced it with the Stormer HVM in the late 1990s. Added in Update 2.45 "Hornet's Sting", it carries eight Mk.1E missiles reaching 7 km or eight Mk.2s reaching 8 km, with a thermal imager for finding aircraft. Protection is limited and the crew is exposed to most kinds of fire.
uk_ttd: South Africa's Loggim programme of the 1980s sought a home-built MBT, and despite budget cuts after the Border War a Tank Technology Demonstrator was completed in 1992, with 282 envisaged as Olifant Mk.1A and Mk.1B replacements; once arms sanctions ended after the 1994 elections, foreign tanks became an option, the project was cancelled and the TTD went to a museum in 1997. Added in the "Ixwa Strike" update, it is conventional but draws on Olifant solutions, with a 1,250 hp engine, a good thermal sight and a 105 mm GT-3 firing DM63 APFSDS. Its size and mediocre armour make urban maps difficult.
uk_valentine_mk_1: Vickers-Armstrongs began the Valentine privately in 1938, drawing on the A9, A10 and A11; the War Office disliked its two-man turret, which made the commander load, but approved it in April 1939 with first deliveries in May 1940. In the game since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", the Valentine I has a quick-firing 40 mm 2-pounder and excellent all-round armour that defeats most opponents when angled, with a turret shape that deflects some hits. It is very slow, topping out at 24 km/h and reversing at just 3 km/h, and has only three crew and low-magnification optics that make long shots difficult.
uk_valentine_mk_11: The Valentine XI rearmed the Mk X with a 75 mm QF gun, used a 210 hp GMC diesel and had welded rather than riveted armour; almost every Valentine mark except the Mk I was supplied to the Soviet Union under Lend-Lease. Present since Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it pairs a hard-hitting 75 mm and a fairly quick reload with excellent armour, which most opponents struggle to penetrate when the hull is angled, while the turret shape deflects some shots. Its turret traverses very slowly, and with a 24 km/h top speed and 2.4 km/h reverse it is extremely sluggish.
uk_valentine_mk_9: One of the original British ground vehicles from Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", the Valentine IX carries the strong 6-pounder, which reliably penetrates many opponents. Its armour is still fairly good, especially the turret cheeks, though the hull is weaker and guns met in uptiers can get through anywhere. Mobility is poor, but a small profile helps it stay unseen.
uk_vfm_5: FMC developed the CCVL as an autoloading Sheridan replacement built from M113 and Bradley parts, and when it was unveiled in October 1985 Vickers proposed a cheaper export version: the VFM5 combined FMC's hull with a Vickers aluminium turret, manual loading and the L7 gun. A prototype was shown in 1986, but no buyers emerged and work stopped in the early 1990s. Added in Update 2.1 "New Power", it is fast enough for aggressive flanking and its L7 reloads quickly, but it has no thermal imager and armour that only stops heavy machine guns.
